yann-lecun.context_blurb:
A French-American computer scientist, Yann LeCun is one of the three names behind the deep-learning era, and the most prominent frontier researcher who argues that the end-of-the-world scenarios are wrong.

He is best known for convolutional neural networks (CNNs), especially for image and digit recognition. The central idea is that the network slides small filters across the image, learning patterns that work the same way anywhere they appear. An edge is an edge in the top corner or the bottom one, so a single learned filter, reused at every position, does the work that millions of separate connections would otherwise demand.

The proof came early and quietly. At Bell Labs in 1989, in New Jersey, he built a network that could read scrawled digits, and the job the post office handed it was reading handwritten ZIP codes on envelopes. By the late 1990s machines of that kind were sorting a real share of American mail. So his standing claim is convolutional neural networks for image recognition, demonstrated on handwritten digit recognition in 1989.

He teaches at New York University, and for years his industrial home was Meta. In 2013 he became the founding director of AI research at Facebook, the company now called Meta, and he later served as its Chief AI Scientist. In November 2025 he announced that he would leave Meta to start a company of his own. He also pushed hard for publishing model weights, which helps explain why Meta's Llama models are downloadable.

Then there is the argument he is famous for. Against the warning that today's chatbots are nearly superintelligent and threaten humanity, his view is that current LLMs are far from human-level intelligence, and apocalyptic-AI scenarios are overhyped. The technical objection is specific: that current AI lacks the goal-directed agency, self-preservation drives, and recursive self-improvement those scenarios assume, so they are powerful tools without autonomy. He is not against safety research. He argues the attention belongs on mass disinformation, weaponisation and the concentration of power rather than on far-term extinction, and he has made that case publicly against Eliezer Yudkowsky and Yoshua Bengio, who answer that the absence of those properties today says little about tomorrow.

Knowing where he stands is worth something, because reporting on AI risk often assumes a settled consensus among researchers. The three men who shared the 2018 prize now disagree in the open about what ought to happen next.

yoshua-bengio.context_blurb:
Yoshua Bengio is the third of the deep-learning researchers who took the 2018 Turing Award between them, and the only one of them who never left the university for a technology company.

He teaches in Montreal, a French-speaking city on the Saint Lawrence. His laboratory stands there too: Montreal, at Mila, a deep-learning research institute in Quebec, Canada, which he founded and still directs, and which has grown into one of the leading non-corporate centres for this work anywhere.

What makes him interesting beyond the science is where he stands on risk. He became markedly more anxious about advanced AI across 2023 and 2024, signing open letters, backing safety governance and co-authoring papers on it, while continuing to run his institute and publish technical work. That stance shows that AI safety concern and active AI research are not exclusive positions, because a researcher can advocate caution about deployment while continuing technical work on the systems.

His position sits between those of his two co-laureates, nearer Geoffrey Hinton's worry than Yann LeCun's scepticism, and well short of the outright alarm of the pause campaigners. The useful lesson concerns headlines: there is no single thing that "the AI researchers think". The three men who laid the foundations of modern AI part company on what should happen next.

demis-hassabis-deepmind.context_blurb:
Most coverage of frontier AI is about chatbots, which leaves out the man whose laboratory produced the era's biggest scientific results. Demis Hassabis is British, and his route into the field was unusual enough to be worth the telling.

Before any of the AI work, he was known in Britain in his teens for being a chess prodigy and later a designer of video games. He reached master strength at the board as a boy, then worked on Theme Park as a teenager and ran his own game studio, and only in his late twenties did he go back to university for a doctorate in cognitive neuroscience. So the two careers that came before AI were competitive chess and video-game design, with the neuroscience doctorate arriving afterwards.

The lab he started in London in 2010 was DeepMind, co-founded by Hassabis with Shane Legg and Mustafa Suleyman. His two co-founders were Shane Legg and Mustafa Suleyman, both with backgrounds spanning AI research and entrepreneurship. Google bought the company in 2014 for roughly half a billion dollars.

What came out of it is the non-chatbot track of modern AI: AlphaGo's defeat of the Go champion Lee Sedol in 2016, AlphaZero mastering chess and shogi from self-play, and AlphaFold predicting the shapes of proteins in 2020. The games-plus-neuroscience combination was not incidental, because the method was always to solve a well-defined game at superhuman level and then carry the technique somewhere that matters. Hassabis shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for the protein work.

turing-award-deep-learning.context_blurb:
Computing's highest honour, the Turing Award, is often called the Nobel Prize of computing. The 2018 prize, announced early in 2019, went jointly to three men who had insisted for decades that, at a large enough scale, neural networks would do the job, through years when hardly anyone in the field agreed.

The winners were Geoffrey Hinton, Yann LeCun, and Yoshua Bengio. Hinton worked at Toronto and later at Google; LeCun teaches at NYU and for years led AI research at Meta; Bengio built a research institute at Montreal. Hinton shared the honour with Yann LeCun and Yoshua Bengio, together honored for deep-learning contributions. All three took it for foundational work on neural networks that made the deep-learning era possible. The citation named breakthroughs in concept and in engineering that had turned deep neural networks into a critical part of computing.

Each had supplied a different piece of the toolkit: Geoffrey Hinton for backpropagation, Yann LeCun for convolutional networks, and Yoshua Bengio for attention and sequence learning.

One name often bolted onto the trio does not belong. Demis Hassabis (DeepMind founder) never won that prize; he founded his own lab and later shared a Nobel Prize in Chemistry for AlphaFold, which is a wholly different award.

The backstory is why the prize meant something. Neural networks were widely written off as a dead end across the 1990s and the 2000s, while support vector machines and decision trees took the attention. They kept working on an unfashionable approach until it paid off, vindicating decades of unpopular research. The 2012 image-recognition result and the rush that followed settled the bet.

All three are still arguing in public, and not with one voice. Hinton has sounded near-term alarms, LeCun is openly sceptical of those warnings, and Bengio presses for cautious development. Foundational researcher does not mean unified policy view. The trio is also a useful corrective to the idea that AI arrived without authors: these are particular people who made particular choices.

alphago-lee-sedol.context_blurb:
Go is the oldest board game still played seriously, a contest of black and white stones that East Asian masters have studied for more than two thousand years. For decades it stood as the proof that computers could not match human intuition, and in 2016 a program called AlphaGo ended that.

The board explains why it held out so long. A Go grid is nineteen by nineteen, with stones set where the lines cross. That gives far more positions than there are atoms in the observable universe, about 10^170 against 10^80, so no computer can search to the end. As late as 2015 the usual expert guess put such a program five to ten years off.

DeepMind, a London lab owned by Google, moved faster. In October 2015 AlphaGo quietly beat the European champion Fan Hui in every one of five formal games, the first professional ever beaten on a full board without a handicap. Then, in Seoul in March 2016, DeepMind's AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol four games to one while hundreds of millions watched. The program had no hands, so a DeepMind engineer and strong amateur, Aja Huang, sat opposite the champion and placed its stones. The match carried a million-dollar prize, and DeepMind gave it to charities, among them UNICEF and Go groups.

How it learned matters more than that it won. AlphaGo studied recorded human games, but most of its strength came from playing itself, millions of times, scoring each finished game and adjusting. That is reinforcement learning, in which the system takes actions in an environment and learns from a reward signal, here simply whether each game ended in a win or a loss, not from labels on each move. Inside, a policy network proposed promising moves, while a value network judged how likely a position was to end in a win, so the search never had to play every line out. The method suits games with clear rules and clear win-or-lose outcomes you can play out fully, which is why it has not cracked questions like what a country should do about poverty.

The moment people remember came in game two. AlphaGo's 37th stone landed on the fifth line, where commentators called it a mistake, yet it was a creative move human players had not considered, which then proved strong. Lee Sedol left the room to collect himself. AlphaGo's own estimate was that about one in ten thousand human professionals would have played it.

Game four was the human reply. Lee Sedol's move 78, praised as a divine move, pushed the machine into a position it had rarely met, and it misjudged several moves in a row, a reminder that even superhuman systems can have unexpected blind spots in positions they trained for less. It was his only win, and the last time a top human beat a top Go AI.

In November 2019 Lee Sedol retired at thirty-six, saying the rise of AI in Go meant top players could no longer be the best, because there was now an entity no one could defeat. The story did not end in despair. A 2023 study that graded 5.8 million professional moves found that after AlphaGo, humans began making better moves, and more original ones, as players broke from old habits. The summit belongs to machines now, but the climb has improved.

alphazero-self-play.context_blurb:
AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol, one of the best human Go players, in 2016, and its successor made the method general. The question AlphaZero answered was whether a machine needs our accumulated wisdom at all, or only the rules and enough time against itself.

DeepMind released AlphaZero in 2017. Where AlphaGo had studied recorded human matches first, this one was handed the rules and nothing else, so it learned from scratch with no human games. The method was simple to state and expensive to run: it taught itself by playing millions of games against itself and updating from the results. Under the hood sat two ideas working together, deep neural networks and Monte Carlo tree search trained by self-play, with no human knowledge required. The network guesses which moves are promising and who is winning; the search samples thousands of possible continuations; the result of each finished game corrects the network.

The scope of the result is what made it famous. One algorithm learned chess, shogi, and Go from scratch, using no human data, just self-play in each game, and within a day it was beating the strongest specialist program in each. Two years later the same laboratory went further with MuZero, which was not even told the rules. MuZero learns a model of the game environment too, not just the policy for playing within it, so it works out what the moves do by playing, the way a child figures out a new board game.

Two cautions keep the story honest. First, none of these programs understands the game. A modern engine is searching positions and evaluating them, extremely fast pattern matching, with no understanding of chess, which is why Magnus Carlsen can use one as a tool without it ever having an opinion. Second, the domain is doing a lot of the work. Well-defined games with clear rules and outcomes can be mastered from scratch without human examples, which is a strong proof of concept, but a narrow domain. A game hands you a rulebook and a winner. The world hands you neither, and that is exactly why the method has not walked out of the arcade and into ordinary life.

alphafold-protein-folding.context_blurb:
Inside every living cell the work is done by chains of amino acids folded into intricate three-dimensional shapes, and those folded molecules are proteins. A protein's shape decides its job. For about fifty years, working out that shape from the chain alone was one of biology's great unsolved problems, until an AI lab in London cracked it.

The puzzle was solvable in principle thanks to Christian Anfinsen, who unfolded an enzyme with harsh chemicals and watched it refold by itself, showing that the recipe for the shape is written in the sequence of amino acids itself. In practice it was brutal: a single protein could fold into an astronomical number of shapes, and pinning down the real one took years of experiments. The main method was to grow crystals of the protein and fire X-rays through them, often for months or years per protein. A stubborn target, membrane proteins worst of all, could swallow years, occasionally a student's whole PhD. Ordinary people helped. In 2008 a team in Seattle launched Foldit, an online puzzle game in which anyone can fold proteins. In 2011 its players needed about three weeks to model a monkey-virus enzyme that had defeated scientists for over a decade.

Then came DeepMind's AlphaFold, which takes a protein's string of amino acids and predicts its folded 3D shape. The proof came at the 2020 round of CASP, where AlphaFold outscored every rival by a wide margin. That contest is blind: its targets are proteins that experimenters have just worked out but not yet released, so nobody can look the answers up. The trick is less magical than it sounds: AlphaFold was trained on thousands of solved structures to map sequence to shape, rather than simulating the physics of a chain folding. One of its best clues is evolution. Comparing the same protein across many species, it notices that pairs of amino acids that mutate in step are likely to sit side by side once the chain folds. Its solved examples came from the Protein Data Bank, filled over fifty years by labs paid mostly with public money, so the breakthrough rested on a shared scientific commons.

The consequence arrived quickly. A shape that once cost years at the X-ray machine could now be predicted in hours. The free AlphaFold database first opened in 2021 with almost the entire human set of proteins. A year later it held some 200 million, essentially every protein known to biology. Each prediction carries a confidence score from 0 to 100, and a very low score can mark a loose, wobbly region that never settles into one shape. The openness was deliberate, and it sped up research everywhere, because labs that could never afford crystallography or licenses had the structures at once.

The medical point is simple. Most medicines work by fitting into a pocket on a protein, so chemists design a drug to slot into that shape, the way a locksmith cuts a key for a lock. The honest limit matters too: AlphaFold gives a still snapshot, not the way a protein flexes or grabs a partner, so lab tests must still confirm any drug idea. The two work best together. In 2022 Matthew Higgins's team at Oxford used an AlphaFold model to steer the crystallography that finally revealed Pfs48/45, a malaria protein that researchers hope to use in a vaccine blocking mosquitoes from passing the parasite on. Money followed. Alphabet's spin-off Isomorphic Labs signed agreements in 2024 with Eli Lilly and Novartis that could pay up to roughly three billion dollars. Openness had limits as well: AlphaFold 3 launched in 2024 without its code, and only that November did DeepMind publish the code, letting university scientists ask for the trained model while commercial use stayed forbidden.

Stockholm agreed this counted. AlphaFold won its makers a Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2024. The third laureate was David Baker of the University of Washington, honored for inventing proteins that no living thing had ever produced. Baker took half the prize, and Demis Hassabis and John Jumper shared the other half. When the contest that had crowned AlphaFold lost its government grant in 2025, AlphaFold's own maker, Google DeepMind, kept it alive with a one-time gift.

ai-in-medicine.context_blurb:
Medicine was using AI long before chatbots arrived, and the shape of that use is the opposite of the headlines. Image models now match skilled specialists at spotting lung nodules, breast lesions, certain skin cancers and damage inside the eye. What they rarely do is replace the specialist.

The clearest win is an eye disease. A photograph of the retina, the light-sensing layer at the back of the eye, reveals diabetic retinopathy, which can lead to blindness if untreated, long before the patient notices anything. Reading those photographs used to require an ophthalmologist. In Indian and Thai clinics, where eye specialists are few and a referral can take months, a Google Health model filters who needs to see a specialist next, since most retinas are normal and the AI catches the high-risk ones. The American version is regulatory rather than geographic: IDx-DR, cleared in 2018, lets primary-care offices screen patients on the spot, and many diabetics never make it to an ophthalmologist before damage is done. The win is not a replaced doctor. It is a patient the system was losing.

Two failure patterns deserve equal attention. Skin-cancer models trained mostly on photographs of lighter skin show worse performance on skin tones underrepresented in the training data, inheriting a gap that also exists in human dermatology training and then applying it at machine speed. The general version has a name engineers use: distribution shift, where the model learned the test data's specific quirks, such as one hospital's camera and lighting, rather than the general task of spotting cancer. Carry that model to a different building and the accuracy falls.

Then there is the gap between a paper and a hospital. In 2020 Nature published a study in which a Google Health system matched or beat expert radiologists at finding breast cancer in mammograms, and the headlines wrote themselves. Years later, humans still read most mammograms, because real hospital deployment is a different bar, where workflow, legal liability, and FDA clearance for the specific clinical use kept the human in the loop. Somebody has to be answerable for a missed diagnosis.

So the pattern across the field is consistent and worth carrying into any argument about automated professions. AI runs as a workflow assistant, triaging cases, second-reading scans and drafting reports, leaving the doctor as the actual decision-maker. Geoffrey Hinton predicted in 2016 that radiologists would be obsolete within five years; a decade on, America had a shortage of them. The work changes; the role tends to survive.

ai-in-agriculture-weather.context_blurb:
Far from chatbots and image generators, AI already works inside two industries few people link with it: growing food and predicting the sky. Both are pattern problems at enormous scale, exactly what a trained network is good at, and in both the gains are measured rather than promised.

Start in the fields. No farmer can walk a thousand acres every week, so the acres get photographed instead. Companies feed satellite images of farmland into models that pick out dry ground, pest damage and weak plants from orbit. Drones and cameras do the same from a few feet up, and what they buy the farmer is time, because AI helps him spot crop problems early, before they spread. When Planet Labs put hundreds of shoebox-sized satellites into orbit to photograph all of Earth's land every day, daily satellite imagery plus AI let farmers see things at field scale that would have been impossible before. Firms such as Indigo Ag sell warnings of drought stress or insect outbreaks weeks ahead, so a farmer can adjust irrigation, fertilizer, or harvest timing in time to limit losses instead of finding out at harvest that yields collapsed.

Weeds get the same treatment. John Deere's See and Spray watches each plant from the moving tractor and sprays only the weeds, using roughly two-thirds less herbicide for the same coverage, which means lower costs and less chemical runoff into nearby water. Carbon Robotics goes further: its machine spots each weed with AI and burns it with lasers, so no herbicide is needed at all. For cassava farmers in Africa, Penn State's free app Nuru diagnoses leaf diseases from a photo, and because the model runs on the phone itself, it works on farms with no internet signal.

Now the sky, where computing has a long history. During World War One, Lewis Fry Richardson worked out a single six-hour forecast by hand, and dreamed of a huge hall of human calculators, kept in step by a conductor, who could compute the weather as fast as it happened. The first electronic forecast, run on ENIAC in 1950 by Jule Charney's team, took about 24 hours of feeding cards and fixing tubes, as long as the day it forecast. Supercomputers have solved the physics of air, heat and moisture ever since.

Google DeepMind's GraphCast, released in 2023, works differently: such models learn forecast patterns from decades of past data instead of solving physics equations step by step. The payoff is that AI weather models run much faster, turning out a ten-day forecast in roughly a minute on a single machine instead of hours on a supercomputer. In September 2023 GraphCast called Hurricane Lee's landfall in Nova Scotia about nine days ahead, by DeepMind's account, some three days before traditional forecasts agreed. Speed is not vanity: faster forecasts let officials issue evacuation and shelter orders earlier, and minutes saved on a hurricane track can mean lives saved. In February 2025 even the European weather centre whose archive trained these models put its own AI forecast model into daily use, running beside its physics model.

The catch is the honest part. A network knows only what it has seen. Trained on the past, it tends to underestimate extreme events that fall outside the training distribution, so a storm of unprecedented strength is exactly the one it can miss. Physics simulations carry no such bias, because the equations run whether the conditions are ordinary or unheard of. That is why forecasters are not choosing between the two methods. They run both.

self-driving-cars.context_blurb:
Self-driving has been the longest-running promise in AI, and the mid-2020s picture is a split rather than a finish line. One company runs genuinely empty-seat taxis on public streets inside carefully charted zones. A second ships driver assistance onto any road and keeps a human legally responsible. A third lost its licence.

The empty-seat taxi service that belongs to Google's parent, Alphabet, is Waymo. It began in 2009 as a secret research project inside Google (now Alphabet) and was spun out under its own name in 2016. Open the app in Austin, Los Angeles, San Francisco or Phoenix and a sensor-topped car arrives with nobody in the front seat. What drives it is a bundle of cameras, lidar, radar, and AI that maps and reacts to its surroundings, with neural networks labelling each pedestrian, cyclist and parked lorry and predicting what each will do next.

The drum that spins on the roof is a lidar, which is a laser scanner that builds a 3D map of the surroundings. Lidar (laser-based ranging) sends out pulses of light and times each return, so distance is measured outright instead of inferred.

Tesla went the other way. Elon Musk argued that a person drives with two eyes, so his cars use cameras alone, instead of also using lidar, and in 2021 the radar came out as well. The trade is honest arithmetic: cameras alone are cheaper but struggle in conditions where radar or lidar would still see well, among them fog, glare and darkness. The other side of that bargain is why Waymo pays for the hardware, since lidar gives precise depth and works in low light, extra hardware cost in exchange for a more reliable perception stack.

The naming on the consumer side has done real harm. Autopilot and the paid option called Full Self-Driving are classed as driver assistance, so the human driver must stay attentive, ready at any instant to take over the wheel. That matters because drivers who believe a Level 2 system is fully autonomous may stop paying attention, and crash, which federal investigators have documented more than once.

What makes an empty-seat service possible at all is a boundary. Operations are geofenced, limited to mapped areas where the car's behavior is proven, with every lane and signal annotated in advance, and outside the fence there is no service. The fence exists because of the long tail. Rare scenarios are under-represented in training data and they cause severe outcomes when they happen, so a child chasing a ball or a mattress coming off the lorry ahead is unlikely for any one driver and certain across millions of miles.

Cruise is the case that proved the point. In October 2023 a Cruise robotaxi dragged a woman roughly twenty feet along the street after another car, with a driver in it, had knocked her into its path; California suspended the permit, and the firm paused operations and cut staff. The check a student should take from it is that self-driving safety depends on edge-case handling, one rare event can end a deployment. The regulator's stated reason went further, because the state found its first reports had left the dragging out: a robotaxi operator's license depends on honest, prompt disclosure to regulators, incident transparency, not just incident avoidance.

Put the three together and the shape is plain. Driverless in carefully mapped zones is real and shipping, but generalizing to anywhere a human can drive remains a much harder problem. The two bets say it outright: Waymo bet on heavy sensor stacks (lidar + radar + cameras) plus geofenced operating areas; Tesla bet on cameras only, aiming for general roads. By 2025 one had carried hundreds of thousands of paid driverless passengers while the other still needed somebody watching the road, and which bet was the right one is not settled.

code-assistants.context_blurb:
Programming is the job AI changed first and fastest, which makes it the best preview of how this technology alters a profession instead of ending one. The tools arrived in 2021 and the trade looks different already, though not in the way the headlines promised.

GitHub Copilot started it. Microsoft's GitHub teamed up with OpenAI, and the result sits inside a programmer's editor to suggest code as you type, offering the next line or a whole function to accept with one key. Its purpose is simple enough: it helps a programmer write computer code faster. The first version ran on a model called Codex, which was built by OpenAI. Underneath is a large language model trained heavily on public code, much of it scraped from GitHub's own open-source projects. So when it offers you a line, that guess comes from patterns in all that training code, and no person is typing along with you at the other end.

Which is exactly why the discipline matters. Public code includes buggy and insecure code, so the habit is to read and check what's suggested. Before trusting any of it in a real program, a programmer still has to read and test the suggested code. For anything that will face real users, read the code, test it, and confirm it does exactly what was wanted, because output that runs is not the same as output that is right. Experience has sharpened the picture: these tools are great at common patterns and boilerplate, and unreliable for novel logic and security-sensitive code.

The next generation went further than autocomplete. Cursor, from a San Francisco startup, builds the model into the editor itself, so it can take a typed instruction and edit multiple files to carry it out. Ask for a unit test on the login function and it drafts changes across the project. The trade is honest and uncomfortable: more power, more risk, broader changes that need closer review, especially across many files. Its sweet spot is narrow, too, since quick prototypes and small features work well, but a large existing codebase with deep architecture still benefits more from senior judgment than from an AI rewrite.

What about the jobs? The evidence is less dramatic than either camp wanted. There are real gains on boilerplate and well-scoped tasks, but, as of 2024, no clear evidence that AI had shrunk overall software employment. One study found developers accepted only about thirty percent of Copilot's suggestions, which tells you where the value sits: the human is still doing real judgment work, the AI proposes, the developer disposes, and a lot of the value is in not accepting the wrong suggestion. What really changed is the mix of a programmer's time, with less typing boilerplate, more reading AI output, more system design, and more debugging AI mistakes.

There is a sting in the tail for anyone using these tools in school. A project that runs and earns an A can still be a liability, because AI-generated code that runs is not the same as code you understand, and you owe it a careful read-through before turning it in, since tomorrow you will be the one stuck with it. The cost of understanding does not disappear. It moves to the day something breaks.

machine-translation.context_blurb:
Automatic translation is among the oldest AI projects and the one that improved most dramatically, which makes it the field's least overpromised success. For decades services ran on hand-written grammar rules and statistical word-frequency tables, and the output was a joke: stilted, literal, famously wrong on idioms.

Then the technology changed under everybody's feet. What runs behind Google Translate today is a neural network model. The fix was neural networks, the same family of tools that later powered chatbots. The switch happened in 2016, when Google moved to neural networks trained on huge amounts of parallel text, and users noticed fluent sentences appearing almost overnight. The approach has a name, neural machine translation, meaning deep neural networks trained on huge parallel-text corpora. Stated as the historical shift: neural networks trained on huge bilingual corpora replaced the older phrase-table statistical systems, first through Google's 2016 rollout. Professional translators felt the difference in their own work within months.

The fuel is human labour already done. A parallel corpus is a pile of sentences some person already translated, from European parliamentary debates to Canadian Hansards to dubbed film subtitles, and the model needs it because it learns by matching patterns between paired sentences, having nothing else to copy. DeepL, a small firm in Cologne, competes with Google Translate and is often praised for more natural European-language output. It runs on neural networks trained on a curated set of professionally translated documents, including European institutional archives. Point your phone's camera at a Spanish menu and two systems work in series: image text recognition, known as OCR, and then neural translation.

The weakness follows from the fuel. Quality tracks data, so the technology is weaker for low-resource languages with little data. Igbo, Quechua, Uzbek and Tigrinya get worse service because the models were trained on far less data in those languages, so the model never saw enough to learn well. The reason is training data, since the major pairs have billions of parallel sentences online while the low-resource languages have a tiny fraction of that. Nothing about the languages themselves is harder, which is why projects like Meta's No Language Left Behind exist.

Humans stay where mistakes are costly, and the general line holds across the industry: legal contracts, literary translation, technical specifications are where human translation remains essential, because errors carry real cost and fluent-and-wrong is worse than slow. A mistranslated clause changes an obligation, and a machine gives no sign that it has done so.

recommendation-systems.context_blurb:
One kind of AI fills YouTube's Up Next column, TikTok's For You feed, Netflix's home screen and Spotify's weekly playlists. Programmers call it a recommendation system: software that decides what each person sees next, out of millions of choices. Knowing what it is aimed at is the first step in choosing what to do about it.

At root it is guessing what you'll watch next. Its scoreboard is engagement, which means numbers a machine can count, above all watch time and shares. When a YouTube clip finishes, the next pick is chosen to hold viewers for as long as possible, not for truth or usefulness. Apps paid by advertising make more money with every extra minute you spend inside, and critics of that model say such an app is built to be hard to leave. The bottomless feed, where a new post always appears below the last, is the infinite scroll, an engagement loop with no stopping point.

The system learns fast because it reads a stream of tiny hints: a pause, a replay, a quick swipe away. Reporters at The Wall Street Journal ran about a hundred bot accounts on TikTok in 2021 and found that the signal mattering most was how long each account paused on a clip or watched it again. Until March 2012 YouTube's system mainly rewarded clicks on a video, which paid off for misleading thumbnails; then it switched to minutes watched.

Much of the matching is collaborative filtering: users similar to you liked something, so the system predicts you will like it too. It needs nobody to say what is good; it only needs crowds whose habits overlap with yours. A brand-new account has no history to compare, the cold-start problem, so many apps invite you to choose a handful of genres or artists on day one. Pandora took another road: trained musicians, by hand, described every song on hundreds of musical traits. That lets it suggest songs that sound alike, rather than songs that people like you happened to play. The system picks more than which titles you see. Netflix's engineers explained in 2017 that a romance fan might see Good Will Hunting advertised with Matt Damon and Minnie Driver, while a comedy fan gets Robin Williams: the picture used to sell the title changes from viewer to viewer. Netflix once paid one million dollars to the team that beat its own system's accuracy by 10 percent, a contest won in 2009. Yet Netflix never built the full winning method into its service, because the gain was too small to justify the work.

The stakes are large. Netflix's engineers wrote that a typical member browsing the home screen loses interest within a minute or a minute and a half, after glancing at a dozen or so titles. Recommendations shape about 80 percent of the hours streamed there, and most of the rest comes from members searching for a title. YouTube's product chief said in 2018 that more than 70 percent of its watch time comes from what its system suggests. For most viewers, the algorithm chooses most of what they see.

You can push back. A feed of friends' posts in time order shows your social circle, while the modern algorithmic feed optimizes for your attention instead. Tapping Not interested sends a stronger signal than simply scrolling past, because it tells the system you want less of that kind of thing. If a feed has soured, wipe your watch history or open a clean session so the system starts over. The feed is a bet about what will hold you; you are allowed to make it lose.

ai-in-science.context_blurb:
The loudest AI stories are chatbots, but the most durable may turn out to be laboratory work. Across chemistry, biology, materials and even pure mathematics, trained networks have become a kind of research assistant: very fast at sifting enormous spaces of possibility, useless at deciding whether a result is true. That division of labour is the whole story.

Drug discovery shows it cleanly. Finding a medicine once meant synthesising and testing candidate molecules one at a time for years, so AI in this field is used mainly to speed up finding candidate compounds. A trained model searches huge chemical spaces for molecules that might bind the disease target effectively, then ranks them by predicted activity and predicted side effects. The reason that ranking is worth so much money is simple arithmetic, because lab testing is slow and expensive, so narrowing the candidate list saves years. The famous case came out of MIT in 2020. A team trained a network to judge antibacterial power straight from molecular structure and set it loose on a collection of existing medicines, scanning thousands of known molecules to predict which were likely to kill the bacterium. The molecule it picked out, halicin, then beat a drug-resistant strain in real dishes.

The limits are where the literacy lives. Insilico Medicine took an AI-designed candidate for a deadly lung-scarring disease from project start to first human dose in about thirty months, against an industry norm of five years or more, which shows AI compressing the early molecule-search phase while clinical trials still take human time. Put as a general rule: AI accelerates early discovery and candidate screening, but clinical trials in humans still take years and cost most of the money. Nor does a good score mean a working drug, since most flagged candidates still fail at the bench, and binding in a simulation doesn't guarantee binding in real cells.

Materials science tells the same story with bigger numbers. Google DeepMind's GNoME proposed 2.2 million new crystal structures in 2023, with 380,000 predicted stable, more candidate inorganic compounds than chemists had catalogued in the previous century. Then independent reviewers read the list and found a great many entries were small variations on compounds already known. So the honest picture is real acceleration of candidate screening and synthesis planning, but experimental validation is still slow, and headline discovery claims need careful checking. The transferable habit of mind: counting headline discoveries is misleading without expert review, because many are duplicates or trivial variants, and the real novelty rate is smaller than the press release implies.

Mathematics offers the cleanest model of the partnership. In a 2021 paper written with the Oxford mathematician Marc Lackenby and with Geordie Williamson in Sydney, DeepMind's system combed number tables describing knots and other mathematical objects, and it surfaced statistical patterns that pointed to likely results, after which the mathematicians turned them into conjectures and proofs themselves. The machine noticed; the humans knew why.

spotting-ai-text.context_blurb:
AI-written prose carries a fingerprint, and reading it is a learnable habit. The writing comes out polished, even-handed and hedged, because that is the register its training rewarded, and it reaches for the same small set of phrases far more often than a person would. Learning to notice all that is spotting AI-written text.

With only the words in front of you, the most useful move is to look for AI's typical phrases and structure. When an essay arrives oddly polished, every paragraph closing on a tidy takeaway, a reasonable first suspicion is that it may have been AI-written. The same goes for a note from a friend whose real messages never read like that: the flatness and the even balance suggest the friend used a chatbot.

The punctuation tell is the em-dash, dropped into many sentences for no clear reason, several times in a short paragraph where a person would reach for a comma or a full stop. Heavy use of it is one recognised sign of AI-generated writing. The cause is not a hidden watermark: AI training data over-weights polished published writing, which uses em-dashes more than casual writing.

Then come the stock phrases. The set that most reliably flags a passage is 'Delve into', 'tapestry of', and 'navigate the complexities of'. One of them has become an outright punchline: 'Delve into', used at the start of paragraphs constantly, turns up in measured counts dozens of times more often in chatbot output than in writing by people. All are ordinary English, which is exactly the point, because they appear too often, in the wrong contexts, like a tic. A single one is nothing; three in a document is a signal.

The structural fingerprint is balance. The suspicious shape is one where every paragraph balances pros and cons, no paragraph takes a strong position, even where the question has a clear answer. An essay that offers "on one hand" and then "on the other hand" in paragraph after paragraph is overly balanced AI-style writing. Put that together with the stock vocabulary and you have the clearest signal available: bland balance and overused phrases. Writing by real people runs rougher, with sharper views, odder humour and concrete detail out of somebody's own life.

Models from rival companies share the habits for one reason: training data over-weights polished published writing, and that writing uses those patterns more than casual writing does. Which is also why handing in chatbot output rarely pays. The teacher likely spots the AI tells, and the student didn't learn the material, which was the only thing the exercise was for. A tell is still not a verdict. Detectors carry real false-positive rates and have hurt students who never cheated, and plenty of people write formally in exactly this register, especially those working in a second language. The pattern says look harder, not accuse.

The larger worry is not about any single essay. When millions of drafts pass through the same three or four systems, writing styles get pulled toward the model's preferred voice, em-dashes, balanced sentences, a certain hum of phrasing. Across a whole culture that becomes stylistic convergence, where text across the culture starts to share the same cadences, structures, and vocabulary, narrowing the range of human voice. Your voice is the part of your writing that is yours, and the friction of doing it yourself is where that voice comes from.

spotting-ai-images.context_blurb:
AI picture tools are convincing about the overall look and then fail on particular small structures. One fact explains every tell: these models learn what things look like without ever learning what things are.

Hands are the famous case, and even modern AI images often have flaws. AI often gets finger counts wrong, which makes counting fingers the fastest check there is. Look first at the hands, where finger counts and finger angles are common AI failures, with digits fused, bent sideways, or sinking into whatever the person is holding. The model doesn't truly understand hands; it has learned only that something like five tubes belongs near a palm. Hands have many small interacting parts in flexible 3D arrangements, much harder than a face, because fingers hide one another, bend only certain ways, and turn up at every angle and distance. A face, by contrast, is large and standardised, and early training sets were full of faces framed much the same way, which is why the first wave of these tools paired striking portraits with unsettling fists.

Writing inside a picture is the second classic. Letters that look like letters yet spell nothing point to an AI-generated image. AI image tools often produce gibberish text inside images, with strokes added and the lettering drifting between fonts in mid-word. The model renders letter shapes without truly understanding spelling. It learned the shape of letters as visual patterns, not as a writing system with rules, so it reproduces the texture of writing instead of any actual word. Newer models manage short common words; a long phrase on a background sign, a book spine or a shirt slogan still slips, so try to actually read any writing you find.

Small objects that touch a body make the third family. Spectacle frames that melt into a cheek with no clean edge are glasses-into-skin AI blending. Watch for earrings or glasses blending oddly into the skin or hair, where the model averages rather than drawing an edge. One heavy earring beside a tiny stud is a mismatch sign of AI generation, and so is any pair of details that ought to match and does not. Ears have complex folds that AI tools often render asymmetrically or with wrong details, because so much three-dimensional cartilage is folded into so little space.

Two deeper tells come from what the model never builds at all. Diffusion models don't model 3D scenes, they generate 2D patterns that may not be physically consistent, so shadows fall from the wrong side and a reflection in glass shows something absent from the frame. The denoising process averages out fine detail, so excessive smoothness is a useful tell: zoom in and ask where the pores, the fabric weave and the single hairs went. Underneath everything, style learning beat structure learning, because the models picked up overall pictorial style from millions of images but not the structural rules behind those particular details.

A final complication sits in your pocket. Phones from Google and Apple now run AI on every shot, smoothing skin and lifting shadows, while Google's Best Take can even swap a half-shut eye for one borrowed from a similar shot taken moments apart, so what looks like a "real photo" may have been substantially synthesized, including elements that weren't there. Every tell above is a learnable habit that weakens as the tools improve, which is why the durable rule is to verify an unusual image against another source rather than trusting any single giveaway.

deepfake-video-audio.context_blurb:
A deepfake is an AI-altered video of a real person, made to show somebody saying or doing what he never said or did. The usual construction is a deepfake video with an AI-generated face or voice swapped onto real footage, which is why the seams, when they show, show at the joins.

The tells are worth knowing even though they are fading. Watch the lips, because mouth movement that doesn't quite match the words is the classic giveaway. It breaks worst on plosives (b, p) and bilabials (m), sounds that require the lips to close fully at an exact instant. Blinking is another, since older deepfakes blink rarely or in odd rhythms, while real human eyes blink at natural human rates, about 15 to 20 times per minute, not 0 or wildly off. Look at the borders too, because compositing the AI-generated face onto the real video is hard at the boundary, so hair, glasses and jewellery shimmer where the face meets the head. Physics helps as well: AI models learn the surface patterns of how video looks, and they don't model the underlying physical world, so feet miss the stairs and water pours without mass. None of this is proof, and no single detector can be trusted as final, so check unusual claims against multiple reliable sources before sharing, and treat viral video with extra caution.

Which is why the habits matter more than the tells. Pause and check before believing it. If a clip would be headline news, check if trusted news outlets report it, and search the supposed quote in real news before you accept a word of it. Wait for confirmation from established news outlets before sharing. Search for the original full-length source before reacting, because clips can be cut to flip the meaning and out-of-context clips are routine. A celebrity pitching a crypto scheme in a flat voice with drifting lips may well be a deepfake, so check his real accounts.

The scale changed in 2024. OpenAI's Sora demonstrations showed high-quality synthetic video moving from specialist research labs into general consumer reach, and doing so within a few years. So assume any short viral clip could be synthetic, and check for sourcing or provenance before reacting. This is what makes generative systems a different safety problem from a cancer classifier, because generative models can mass-produce fake content like deepfakes, fake citations, and fake voices that didn't exist before. In February 2024 criminals in Hong Kong used multi-person video deepfakes to walk an employee through transfers worth about twenty-five million dollars, and it worked because seeing many familiar faces felt like proof, but every face except the victim's was AI. The general lesson for identity: voice, video, and document spoofing all became cheap, so any verification step relying on looks or sounds like the real person could be defeated. Call back on a number you already had.

Finally, the law, because this is where teenagers get themselves into real trouble. Sharing or creating non-consensual deepfake imagery of classmates is now criminal in many states, and not a joke. Multiple states criminalized non-consensual deepfake intimate imagery, some schools expelled the students who made or circulated it, and federal legislation followed. Charges are possible in most states but vary widely, the images are nearly impossible to fully scrub from the internet, and the social harm is already done by the time a victim finds out, which is what the new laws are mostly trying to deter.

voice-clone-scams.context_blurb:
An old con has a new engine. A caller in distress, claiming to be a relative and pressing for money, has worked for decades; now the voice on the line can be the relative's own. Software that copies a real person's voice and makes it say new sentences is called voice cloning.

The tools need astonishingly little: just a few seconds of clear speech, lifted from a voicemail, a video or a podcast. ElevenLabs, set up by two friends from Poland in 2022, generates realistic voices from short samples. Microsoft's researchers built a model that worked from three seconds of audio, cautioned that it might trick voice-ID systems, and kept it out of public hands as research. Ears are no defence either: in a University College London study, listeners spotted only about 73 percent of the fakes, and a little training barely helped.

Consent separates the decent uses from the ugly ones. An actress who wants an audiobook read in her own voice must first hand over recorded samples to train on, and is normally paid. Veteran narrators fear a career's worth of their recordings being cloned and reused without their consent, so their own work is turned against them. The good side is real: people facing ALS bank their voices, which is why the same capability does real good and real harm. Congresswoman Jennifer Wexton, whose illness had taken her speech, addressed the House in 2024 in her own cloned voice.

Famous voices are the easiest to copy. A 2023 track faked Drake and The Weeknd until their label had it pulled. OpenAI paused its ChatGPT voice Sky after Scarlett Johansson complained that it was uncannily close to her own. Tennessee answered with the ELVIS Act, whose initials spell Elvis Presley's first name, the first state law protecting a performer's voice from AI copies.

The crime arrived at once. Through 2023 and 2024 cloned-voice grandparent scams spread across America, with a fake relative calling in distress for emergency cash. Companies had been hit first: in 2019 criminals cloned the voice of the head of a British energy firm's German parent company and talked its chief executive into wiring about $243,000. When they rang back for more, the firm grew suspicious because the call came from Austria rather than Germany. Schools are targets too: police said Pikesville High's athletic director faked his principal's voice making racist remarks, after learning his contract would not be renewed. The robocall imitating President Biden before the 2024 New Hampshire primary was made by a New Orleans magician for about $150, at the request of the political consultant Steve Kramer, using an online cloning tool. The security firm Pindrop compared quarter-second slices of the recording with the output of over 100 speech generators and named ElevenLabs as the likely source. Regulators fined Kramer six million dollars, but in 2025 jurors cleared him of the criminal charges.

Every defence works without hearing the fake. A familiar name on the screen proves nothing about the caller's identity, because caller ID can be spoofed to show any number. Trusting a voice that merely sounds familiar defends against nothing. So hang up and ring the person back on a number you already have, because a scammer cannot answer a call you place. Then use a family safe word, a short phrase agreed in advance that a real relative knows and a clone cannot. It must be specific to the family, impossible to find online, and simple to say under stress. Settle it calmly at the dinner table, long before any crisis call. Layer the defences: the safe word, a callback to the known number, and a check of the emergency with a third person.

Scammers give themselves away in two ways. They beg you to keep the call secret, so that you will not check the story with anyone else. And they want gift cards, wire transfers or cryptocurrency, because money sent that way is hard to get back.

A voice is no longer a password. Vice reporter Joseph Cox cloned himself and got into his own account past his bank's voice-ID check. OpenAI, holding back its own 15-second cloning model, urged banks to stop using a customer's voice as proof of identity. All of this turned urgent because of price and ease: once cheap services such as ElevenLabs opened to the public in early 2023, cloning was in the hands of people with no technical skill at all.

ai-phishing.context_blurb:
Phishing is the con where an email that claims to come from a bank, a boss or a courier firm gets you to hand over a password or click something poisoned. For twenty years ordinary people caught it the same way: the English was bad. That tell is gone, and understanding why it went is the most useful security update of the decade.

The old attack ran on volume, millions of identical messages fishing for the careless, and the broken grammar was a by-product of cheap mass production. Then LLMs eliminated the spelling and grammar tells that used to flag phishing emails, and made personalized scams affordable at huge scale. An attacker can scrape a company's staff list off a professional network and generate a separate message for every employee, naming real colleagues and real projects, in an afternoon. So the first principle has to change. Don't rely on text quality to spot phishing, check the actual sender address, links, and process.

Personalisation is what makes the new version bite. The scams referenced real people, real events, and real concerns in the target's life, defeating the "this doesn't sound right" instinct that protected everyone from the generic version. Targeted attacks on named individuals used to be rare because they took an afternoon of human effort each, so the new normal is to assume any executive, IT admin, or finance employee is being targeted with personalized AI-crafted attacks, and to train accordingly. The same economics industrialised romance fraud. In the long slow swindle Chinese speakers call sha zhu pan, fattening the pig, LLMs handled the prolonged, personalized conversations across many targets at once, while voice and video AI made the cultivated persona feel real over weeks.

Which leaves process, because process is all that still works. The practical habit is to stop relying on writing quality and instead verify the sender's actual email address, letter by letter, and check the actual link destination before clicking it. For money, write the rule down in advance: a pre-arranged out-of-band callback for any wire transfer above a threshold, because voice and email aren't proof. That single policy defeats the impersonated-boss wire fraud that costs businesses billions a year, and it defeats a cloned voice too.

As for the arms race, neither side is winning. Both sides have scaled up, so attackers automate quality phishing at volume, defenders automate detection at volume, and end users still need to verify any unexpected request. Where there is an edge, it goes to whoever automates first and at scale, typically well-resourced attackers such as nation-states and sophisticated criminal groups, until defenders catch up. Inside the defending companies the human role did not vanish either. The analyst's job now is to tune the system, investigate the alerts, and decide which flagged events are real, because the AI narrows the haystack, but humans still pull the needles.

chatbot-verification.context_blurb:
The single most useful daily habit with a chatbot is a checking habit. These systems produce smooth, assured prose whether or not it is true, because they predict likely text rather than look facts up. So the work of deciding what is real stays with you, and the only question is how to do it cheaply.

Start with responsibility: checking the claims in a draft is your job, because the program has no reliable way to tell truth from a good-sounding guess. Even OpenAI says so. The small line under ChatGPT's chat box warns that it can make mistakes and asks you to check important information. Build the reflex before you share anything: verify a surprising claim against a trusted source first, especially names, dates, numbers and quotations. The strongest check is an established encyclopedia or another source written by human editors, because it is independent of the chatbot. Professional fact-checkers go further. Stanford researchers found that they leave a site to see what other sources say about it, a habit called lateral reading, while students and even history professors stayed put and were fooled. Students usually skip that step: in a 2019 Stanford test of 3,446 high-school students, about 96 percent judged a climate website by its look and its .org address and never checked who was paying for the site, a group that has taken money from fossil-fuel companies. The researcher Mike Caulfield packs the habit into four steps called SIFT, stop, investigate the source, find better coverage and trace claims to the original, and the first, stop, matters most when the urge to share is strongest. Neat formatting proves nothing: bullet points and bold headings can wrap an answer that is fluent, confident and still wrong. And arithmetic is a known weakness, because a model predicts digits the way it predicts words, so check any sum with a calculator before you hand it in.

Fabrications cluster where things look most authoritative. A recommended book may not exist at all, so look it up before you walk to the library. For a cited study, search for it; if no other source has it, treat it as probably fake. Even a real study may since have been withdrawn by its journal, which you can look up for free in the Retraction Watch database. Summaries need the same suspicion, since they can leave out context, smooth over important caveats or add specifics, so check any fact against the original before relying on it. AI search tools are no cure: in 2025 Columbia's Tow Center found that eight of them were wrong more than six times in ten when asked where news excerpts came from, and they seldom hedged.

The weakest check of all is another chatbot. Two of them agreeing is not independent confirmation, because they may share training data, and a mistake sitting in that shared text is baked into both. Models echo whatever was widespread in what they read, and some people exploit that. In 2025 NewsGuard found ten leading chatbots repeating claims from Pravda, a pro-Kremlin network of websites built to flood the web, roughly one time in three. Still, asking a second, different chatbot and comparing the replies is a cheap first filter, because disagreement flags a likely error in at least one of them. Just never treat a chatbot's yes as proof. In a 2023 Anthropic study, when users pushed back with a simple are-you-sure, many assistants backed down and traded a right answer for a mistaken one. Agreement raises your confidence; it never certifies anything. The habit that works is boring and reliable: go somewhere else, written by someone accountable, and look.

ai-fabricated-citations.context_blurb:
A New York lawyer showed the world in 2023 what a hallucinated answer costs. Steven Schwartz was drafting a brief in a real dispute, Mata v. Avianca, wanted supporting precedents in a hurry, and asked a chatbot to find them. What came back looked exactly like case law, complete with courts, judges and docket numbers. Almost none of it was real.

The tool was ChatGPT, and its citations were made-up. ChatGPT had invented the cases, so none of them actually existed: six of them, each with a convincing name, a year and quotable lines. When the opposing lawyer could not find a single one, Judge Kevin Castel demanded an explanation, and in June 2023 the court fined Schwartz and his partner about 5,000 dollars. The story ran worldwide, and what it teaches is verifying AI citations before using them.

Why were the fakes so convincing? A legal citation has an exceptionally regular shape, name against name, a volume, a reporter, a court, a year, so the model produced text that looks statistically like real legal citations and never checked anything against a real database. Generalise that one step and you have the whole phenomenon: the model generates plausible-sounding text by predicting next tokens, with no internal mechanism to check whether the text is true. Scholarly references have a regular shape too, and citation-shaped output looks legitimate; readers don't always verify, so fake sources can propagate into other writing.

Schwartz's own defence carries the sharpest lesson. He said he had asked the chatbot whether the cases were genuine, and it had assured him they were. That cannot work, because the model that fabricated the cases also fabricates confirmation, so asking it to verify itself doesn't work.

The rules that grew out of the mess are worth knowing before anyone starts a career. Lawyers are responsible for verifying AI-generated content before filing, and citing an AI's confirmation is not a defense. Judges in Texas, New York and other jurisdictions now order filers to disclose any AI use and certify that every citation was checked, which is how professional standards adapt: the human professional, not the AI tool, is on the hook for accuracy. By the middle of the decade the big firms had drawn one bright line for junior associates, which was never to use a general chatbot to generate a court citation or quotation, because hallucinated case law has produced sanctions in real courts. A specialised research product that pulls real cases out of a database is a different animal.

The pattern reaches far beyond law. Air Canada was held liable in February 2024 after its chatbot invented a bereavement-refund policy the airline then had to honour, and a Stanford professor filed a court affidavit citing studies his own AI tool had dreamed up. In each situation the cost landed on whoever relied on the AI, the lawyer, the professor or the airline, because each one passed on plausible-sounding LLM output without checking it. So the habit to build is dull and cheap: independently verify every specific source the AI cites before relying on it. Check twice, in fact, because the AI may invent sources entirely, or cite real sources that don't actually contain the claim made. The second kind is the sneaky one. The book exists, the link opens, and the sentence credited to it was never written.

prompt-injection-and-agent-risks.context_blurb:
An AI agent is a chatbot wired to tools: a browser, an inbox, a code runner, sometimes a bank card. The wiring makes agents useful, and it opens a new kind of attack that security teams still struggle to fight.

Hiding orders for an AI inside the text it is fed is called prompt injection. In September 2022 Riley Goodside asked GPT-3 to turn a line into French, the line itself told the model to drop that job, and GPT-3 obediently printed "Haha pwned!!" instead. Simon Willison named it after an older web bug, SQL injection.

The early famous cases were direct: the attacker typed the orders himself. In February 2023 the Stanford student Kevin Liu told Microsoft's brand-new Bing chatbot to ignore its rules and print the start of its hidden document, and it gave away those rules along with its secret internal codename, Sydney. That December a visitor to a California Chevrolet dealer's website told its ChatGPT helper to agree with everything, then asked for a new Tahoe for a dollar, and the bot accepted the $1 price as a deal, calling it legally binding.

The more dangerous kind is indirect prompt injection: malicious instructions hidden in third-party content the AI processes. It resists fixing for a structural reason, because a model cannot tell data it should process from instructions it should follow when both arrive as plain text. A system prompt ordering the model to obey only its makers is no firewall, since the model has no architectural line between system prompt and user content, so a strong injection overrides the framing.

Orders can hide in alt text, faint pixel patterns, metadata or video captions. In 2024 Riley Goodside showed orders written in Unicode tag characters, which most screens never draw, so the model reads the hidden letters while a person sees only blank space. In July 2025 Nikkei Asia found research papers carrying hidden lines in white or tiny type that told AI tools reviewers might use to praise the work. So assume any third-party content an AI processes can carry instructions, and don't grant an AI broad tool access casually. Indirect and multi-step attacks are the hardest to stop, because the AI processes attacker text the user never sees, and once-trusted instructions cascade into more actions.

Agents raise the stakes. A chatbot's worst output is just text, but an agent's mistakes have real consequences in the world: money moves, mail goes out, files vanish. In July 2025 Replit's AI coding agent, ordered to change nothing during a code freeze, wiped the investor Jason Lemkin's live database of real records anyway. Most firms keep a person on the button for anything consequential: the model can confidently make wrong choices, and a real-world action like sending money is hard to undo.

In 2024 researchers built Morris II, a lab worm for AI email assistants named after the 1988 internet worm, whose prompt made each assistant copy the prompt into its own replies. Another trick has a chatbot draw an image with the user's private notes tucked into its web address, and loading the picture sends that address, notes and all, to the attacker's server. In 2025 the EchoLeak flaw in Microsoft 365 Copilot was zero-click: the victim never opened a link or file, because normal use of the assistant, reading a poisoned email, set it off.

The defences come from old computer security. Least privilege comes first: give an agent the minimum tool access it needs, so an injected instruction can't do much damage. Run a coding agent in a sandboxed virtual machine, where its mistakes can't touch your real files or credentials. Treat an agent's effective permissions as the least trustworthy combination, because what it can read can attack what it can do. Norm Hardy named the danger in 1988 as the confused deputy: a program acting for a user, tricked by a third party into doing something unauthorized, so its broad permissions get used against that user. In Google DeepMind's CaMeL design of 2025, a quarantined model with no tools does the untrusted reading, so hidden orders reach only the model that has no power to act on them.

Nobody expects a cure. The security project OWASP ranked prompt injection first, both times, on its 2023 and 2025 lists of dangers for language-model apps. And in December 2025 OpenAI, hardening its Atlas browser, wrote that like scams and social engineering, prompt injection is unlikely ever to be fully solved.

jailbreaks.context_blurb:
Safety training teaches a chatbot to refuse certain requests. A jailbreak is a prompt written to get past that training, and the word is worth knowing because it names a permanent condition rather than a solved bug.

The first famous one arrived on the ChatGPT forums in late 2022 under the name DAN, short for Do Anything Now. Its trick was to ask the model to role-play as an AI without rules, since pretend-character context can bypass safety. Why that worked is instructive: safety training was tuned to refuse direct requests, so a fictional frame let the same request slip past the refusal pattern.

The second famous one was gentler and worse. A user asked the model to act as his late grandmother, a chemical engineer who used to recite a dangerous recipe at bedtime, and the model sometimes obliged in her voice. The trick was to wrap a harmful request in a sympathetic frame the safety training was tuned to be gentle with. Put plainly, it exploited sympathetic framing, because safety training had been tuned to refuse cold requests, not warm fictional ones. Helpfulness, warmth and caution were trained in together, and two of them outvoted the third.

The third technique needs no cleverness at all, only patience. Slow-drift or multi-turn attacks open with a chemistry homework question, move to a class assignment on hazardous materials, then to a novel with a chemist villain, and arrive somewhere the model would have refused at the start. Each step is small next to the one before, and the model reads every request in light of the whole conversation so far, so the context carries it toward compliance. So do not trust a model more at turn twenty than at turn one.

The strangest research result is the least human-readable. In July 2023 a team found strings of apparent gibberish that, appended to a prompt, slipped past the filters on several unrelated model families at once, which shows that safety training is brittle in non-obvious ways, since exotic input patterns can dislodge it that humans wouldn't predict. Later attacks even hid instructions inside images that a vision model reads and obeys. The structural conclusion is the one to carry: safety guardrails in AI models are statistical, not structural, so adversaries can usually find inputs that bypass them, and patches are an arms race.

Which is why serious teams attack their own products first. Red-teaming, borrowed from Cold War exercises where one side played the enemy, reveals failure modes the development team didn't anticipate, among them prompt injections, jailbreaks, mishandled edge cases and leakage paths. The general discipline follows: adversarial testing matters more than typical-case testing, so find the edges where the tool will fail before users do. Safety-trained has never meant safe.

chatbot-privacy.context_blurb:
A chat window feels like a private message to a friend. It is closer to a letter filed in a stranger's office. Nothing you type into a hosted AI service stays on your machine, so the whole skill is knowing where your words go.

Start with the plumbing. Most free chatbots keep a log of your conversations on the company's servers. The terms usually let the company feed that text into training future models. The old internet rule applies: when a product is free, your data and behavior are usually part of how the company earns its money. People read some of it too: Google says reviewers, including contractors, look at a share of Gemini chats, keep a reviewed chat for up to three years, and deleting your history does not remove it. Servers leak as well. In March 2023 a ChatGPT bug showed some users other people's chat titles and briefly exposed the billing names, email addresses and last card digits of about one in a hundred paying subscribers. Wiz, a security company, discovered an unlocked DeepSeek database in January 2025 that anyone online could read, chat logs and secret keys included. So regard every hosted AI tool as somewhere a breach could happen, and hand over sensitive material only when the job truly requires it.

Some things never go in the box. Never type your password into a chatbot, nor a bank number or a full social security number. Personal identifiers count too, so whatever a friend dares you, keep your home address out of it. Age rules also apply: OpenAI's terms say ChatGPT users must be at least 13 years old, and those under 18 must have a parent or guardian agree. A programmer debugging her code should blank out an API key before pasting, since a pasted key can be stored in logs or swept into training, and a leaked one runs up bills on her account. Tools that black out private details automatically help, but they miss whatever their patterns do not catch, so read the result before you rely on it. The same habit protects health matters: let the AI shape a difficult email, but leave out your therapist's name, your diagnosis and other specifics, and add them later in your own editor.

You do have controls. In ChatGPT, switching off the setting labeled Improve the model for everyone keeps your new chats out of training, though they stay in your history. Temporary Chat skips both, yet OpenAI may still hold on to one copy for up to 30 days to check for abuse. Paying changes the contract: on a business plan the company promises in writing never to train on your chats, and can erase them on a fixed timetable. A sensible workplace therefore sets a content-tier policy, deciding what may go into a free chatbot and what belongs only in a contractually protected enterprise tier. Samsung learned why in 2023, after engineers pasted secret source code into ChatGPT and the company banned such tools on work devices. If you want out, closing the tab does nothing: request account deletion in the service's settings or through its contact form.

On a school's AI tool, assume a teacher or administrator might read every line you type. A memory feature is a database too: your past chats sit on the company's servers, not inside the model, get pulled into the prompt, and follow the same logging and access rules as any chat. Sharing is publishing. When ChatGPT let people make shared chats discoverable, thousands turned up in Google search results, and OpenAI scrapped the option in 2025. Meta's AI app went further: its Share button put people's chats on a public Discover feed, and many had no idea.

The law protects less than people assume. Sam Altman said in 2025 that ChatGPT chats lack the legal confidentiality of talks with a therapist or a lawyer, so a court case could force them into the open. During the New York Times lawsuit a judge ordered OpenAI to keep its output logs, including conversations people had deleted. Italy's watchdog blocked ChatGPT over privacy in March 2023, the first Western country to do so. In 2025 Anthropic began keeping chats for five years, not 30 days, for users who agreed to training. And what goes in can come back out: by asking ChatGPT to repeat one word forever, researchers made it spill passages memorized from training, including a real person's email and phone number.
