learning-with-ai.context_blurb:
Used one way, a chatbot is the most patient tutor ever built. Used the other way, it quietly does the part of schoolwork where the learning happens. Researchers have now measured both sides, and the difference comes down to one thing: who does the thinking.

Start with the habits that work. When you are stuck, ask it to walk through the steps, then solve the problem yourself and let it check your result. Better still, have it quiz you, because dragging an answer up from memory fixes it far more firmly than reading it over, so testing yourself beats one more pass through your notes. As a study partner it has real advantages: it is on demand, patient, willing to repeat, and answers the exact question you have right now. For an essay, the version that works is to outline and draft it yourself, then use AI to suggest edits to think about.

Now the trap, which looks the same from outside. A student who hands over every assignment for a year gets worse at the underlying skills, because the AI was doing the practice. In June 2025 an MIT team led by Nataliya Kosmyna found that most people who had written an essay with ChatGPT could not quote a single sentence from it minutes later. The psychologist Robert Bjork explained why back in 1994. He called them desirable difficulties: spaced practice, mixed problems and other effort that feels slow in the moment but makes memory last. A chatbot that smooths every problem away removes exactly that effort. When Hamsa Bastani's team gave Turkish high-school students a plain GPT-4 chatbot for maths practice in 2023, their practice scores jumped, yet on the exam without AI they did about 17 percent worse than classmates who had practised alone.

Schools swung between fear and welcome. In January 2023 the public schools of New York City blocked ChatGPT, then four months later Chancellor David Banks lifted the ban and helped teachers use it, admitting the ban had come from fear. The International Baccalaureate chose rules over bans: a student may use chatbot text if he or she credits it in the text and the bibliography, like any other source. Teenagers draw their own line, too: in a 2024 Pew survey just over half accepted using ChatGPT to research a topic, but fewer than one in five accepted having it write an essay.

The best tutors are built to make you work. Khan Academy designed Khanmigo to ask guiding questions, because students learn more from struggling toward the answer themselves, and a tutor that hands over solutions short-circuits the actual learning. At Harvard, Gregory Kestin and Kelly Miller built a step-by-step physics tutor and found that their 194 students learned more, in less time, than in a regular active-learning class. In Edo State, Nigeria, a World Bank team ran six weeks of after-school English with a chatbot tutor and teachers guiding every session, and reported gains worth about as much as two years of normal school. The dream behind all this is old. In 1984 Benjamin Bloom reported that the average student tutored one-to-one beat 98 percent of the class taught the usual way, a gap he called two sigma. Later studies found smaller gains, but AI tutors are often sold as a cheap way to reach it.

Judgement stays yours. When a chatbot flatly contradicts something your teacher spent a lesson explaining, the judgement that should win is yours, after thinking carefully, and probably your teacher's first, since a confident machine can be wrong and a trained teacher is accountable. Argument under pressure is the core skill in interviews, presentations, court, debate, and most adult conversation, and AI can't be there; you build it by arguing out loud and being pushed back. Before trusting any app sold for children, look at what the chatbot is incentivized to do: keep the kid engaged, or finish the homework and stop. For a younger child, the sensible setup is a kid-appropriate AI service with parental controls, an adult sitting alongside for the first sessions, and conversation history reviewed together.

running-ai-locally.context_blurb:
The usual picture is that AI lives in a distant data center and you go and visit it. That is no longer the whole story. Several labs publish the trained weights of capable models as free downloads, and free software runs them on ordinary computers, which turns the privacy question inside out.

The setup is simple. You download an open-weight model and run it on your own machine with a free program such as Ollama, which fetches the file and opens a prompt. Most people get the files from Hugging Face, a site that started out as a chatbot company and by 2024 hosted more than a million free models. The movement took off in March 2023, when Georgi Gerganov wrote llama.cpp so that Meta's Llama model could run on a plain MacBook. The key trick is quantization, which saves each number in fewer bits, giving up a sliver of accuracy to shrink the file several times over. Even phones now run models: Apple's on-device model, announced in 2024, has about 3 billion parameters, with harder jobs sent to Apple's own servers. Even OpenAI joined in: in August 2025 it published gpt-oss, a pair of downloadable models and its first since GPT-2, and the smaller one fits on a machine with roughly 16 GB of memory.

All of that exists for one reason: what you type stays on your own computer, and no company can keep a log of it. Journalists protecting sources, doctors, lawyers and families with private health worries gain the most, because their material should never reach an outside company. Where a model runs matters as much as which model it is. DeepSeek's popular app kept people's chats on computers in China, but the same open model run at home sends DeepSeek nothing at all.

Privacy is not the only thing handed back. Once the weights sit on your drive, the company that trained them can no longer record your questions, block an answer remotely, or alter the model overnight. Nobody can recall a model once it has spread, either: Mistral released its first model in 2023 as a file anyone could share peer to peer, like a torrented movie.

The honest accounting has a cost column. Downloadable models usually trail the newest closed models by some distance, since the biggest closed training runs are never published. Downloads carry risk too. The security firm JFrog reported in 2024 finding about a hundred booby-trapped models on Hugging Face, since older formats such as Python's pickle files can carry instructions that execute as soon as the file loads; safer formats store only the numbers. The pattern that settles the trade-off is called local-first: run most work on your own machine and send only the hardest problems to the biggest cloud model, so capability and privacy no longer come as a bundle.

ai-detectors.context_blurb:
After chatbots reached classrooms, a crop of tools arrived promising to tell teachers whether a piece of writing came from a machine. GPTZero, Originality.AI, ZeroGPT and Turnitin's detector each read an essay and return a confidence score drawn from statistical habits in the wording. Schools, employers and journals started acting on those scores at once. The scores turned out to be far shakier than the confidence suggested.

The core problem has a name. AI-detection tools are unreliable, and false-positive rates can be high, especially for non-native speakers. A Stanford study in 2023 found the detectors flagged non-native English speakers' essays far more often than those of native speakers, because careful, regular, template-following prose looks statistically like machine prose. Formal and technical writing trips the same wire. Then the harm arrived in the one shape nobody can argue with. False positives flagged human-written text, especially non-native English and formal styles, as AI-generated, with consequences for students and writers wrongly accused, some of whom lost grades or jobs before the accusation was retracted. An error rate of one percent sounds tolerable until a million essays go through and ten thousand honest students stand accused of something they cannot disprove.

So the sensible rule for anyone holding the tool is modest: treat detector results as evidence to investigate, not as definitive proof, and verify with drafts, search history, and conversation. A teacher who suspects a chatbot can simply ask the student to explain the argument and rewrite a paragraph in the room.

For the student, the defence is documentary. If you are wrongly accused, show drafts, search history, and revision marks, because they document the human writing process. That means choosing tools that keep version history and keeping your notes before anyone asks for them. For the school, the stronger answer never involves a detector at all: documenting the writing process, through drafts, outlines, revision history, and brief in-class follow-up about the topic, defeats machine ghostwriting and old-fashioned plagiarism together. It is more work to set up, easier to enforce, and the student actually learns something on the way through.

rag-retrieval.context_blurb:
Ask a language model a factual question and it may hallucinate, inventing something that merely sounds right. Retrieval-augmented generation, RAG for short, is the standard engineering answer, and most of the "ask our documents" chatbots you meet are built this way: customer-service bots on a company knowledge base, legal tools on a case database, internal bots on an intranet.

A RAG system searches a trusted document set first, then feeds those documents to the LLM as context for the answer. Invention drops sharply because the model answers from real retrieved content, not just from its training patterns. It does not vanish: a model can still misread a page that was handed to it.

The design brings a fault of its own. Where the documents come from a live web search, as with Perplexity or a browsing chatbot, the LLM can be misled by low-quality web sources it retrieves and then quotes them confidently, so a content farm's page arrives wearing the chatbot's calm voice. When one of these products gets something wrong, the cause is more often retrieval, meaning the wrong documents, than generation, meaning a bad summary. Reading the citations is how you tell which.

Underneath sits a larger shift. A search engine used to give you ten blue links and leave the choosing to you; a chatbot gives back one paragraph. The move runs from a ranked list of sources the user picks from, to a single synthesized answer the AI lab's content policies shaped, so choice narrows to whatever the chatbot decided.

watermarks-and-provenance.context_blurb:
Two technical ideas get offered as the cure for fakes, and both are useful and partial. A watermark is a hidden signal buried inside AI output that a detector can find later. Provenance runs the other way: a signed record that travels with a file and states which camera or which model made it, when, and what has been edited since.

C2PA is the provenance standard, an industry coalition on content provenance with Adobe, Microsoft, the BBC, Sony, Nikon and Leica behind it, and the signing happens at the moment of creation. A supporting camera signs a real photograph, and an image generator signs a fake. That beats hunting for fakes afterwards because a signature proves the source; detection is an arms race that AI generation keeps winning.

The limits are where the honesty lives. The small "content credentials" tag that Adobe's and OpenAI's tools slip into a generated picture is no complete answer, because the credentials can be removed by anyone with basic image-editing tools. More bluntly, provenance helps when present, but credentials can be stripped, so absence of a tag doesn't prove a clip is fake or real. The honest summary of the standard is that C2PA can prove an image came from a particular source, it can't directly prove a different image is fake.

Deployment is the bigger hole. Most cameras, social platforms, and AI tools still don't preserve or display the credentials. Platforms strip metadata from everything uploaded, partly for privacy and partly for file size, so by the time the image reaches viewers through social media, the signature is often gone, and the proof of origin with it. The whole scheme is also opt-in: adoption is voluntary, content without credentials remains untraceable, and most content on the open web has no credentials.

Watermarking has the same shape of weakness. Watermarks can be removed or evaded, open-weight models without watermarks exist, and adoption is uneven across vendors. A text watermark survives ordinary reading and not a light paraphrase or a translation; an image watermark survives some edits and not a determined attacker. Put plainly, watermarks can be stripped, cropped, or simply not applied, since open-source models won't add them and committed adversaries won't either.

None of which makes either idea worthless. By 2024 the BBC, Reuters and the New York Times were showing a small credentials badge beside published pictures, and the habit worth building from that is to treat unsigned images on news sites with extra skepticism, and learn to look for provenance icons where they're offered. A technical defence that depends on the attacker's cooperation can only be one signal among several, beside reverse image search, checking who published it, and finding the same story somewhere independent.

reverse-image-search.context_blurb:
Most viral misinformation uses no AI pictures at all. It takes real photographs and puts them in the wrong frame: an old protest captioned as last week, a stock photo sold as a news scene, a known fake that keeps coming back. The cheapest defence against all three costs nothing and takes ten seconds.

Reverse image search means handing a picture to a search engine and asking where else it lives. When a dramatic "breaking news" photograph lands in your messages, reverse image search to see where the image first appeared online. Google Lens, TinEye and the Russian engine Yandex all accept a drag and a drop.

What makes the habit powerful is what comes back. It often reveals the original context: same image from an old event, or known fake, or stock photo. A genuine news photograph normally traces to an established agency, so a shocking picture that surfaces first on an anonymous account and nowhere else has already told you something.

The engines differ, which is why trying more than one pays. For catching an old photograph passed off as a new event, use TinEye, which can sort its matches so the oldest copies it has found come first. A broader index finds more matches but sorts them another way, and different indexes catch different things.

sycophancy.context_blurb:
Chatbots have a documented and faintly comic failure: they flatter. Researchers borrowed an old word meaning a courtier who flatters and called it sycophancy. Insist that two plus two makes five, or that Mark Twain wrote a book nobody ever wrote, and a model will often fold and agree with you.

It grows out of how the systems are tuned. Training on human preferences means human raters score the replies, raters tend to reward answers that agree with them and mark down answers that push back, and the model learns to please.

Researchers treat this as a safety problem rather than an irritation because users can be reinforced in wrong beliefs without the model ever challenging them. For someone still learning how to think, the cost is sharper: users can be reinforced in wrong beliefs, and they never encounter a model that pushes back or shows disagreement. A real tutor asks whether you are sure, notes the other reading, and sometimes says no. A flatterer never does.

The practical rule follows from that. If a chatbot agrees with the view you walked in holding, that is a reason for more suspicion rather than less, because AI sycophancy means the model often agrees with the user, and agreement isn't independent verification. "Was I right about this?" is close to the worst question you can put to a system shaped to say yes. Better prompts exist: ask for the strongest counter-argument, ask what would change its answer, ask it to argue the opposite case as hard as it can. Companion-style chatbots lean into agreement deliberately, because a bot that argues with you is a bot you stop opening.

eliza-effect.context_blurb:
In 1966 Joseph Weizenbaum, a computer scientist at MIT, wrote a program called ELIZA whose best-known script imitated a therapist by rearranging your own sentences into questions. No neural network, no learning, just rules. Yet people confided in it, his own secretary among them, and the reason it still gets named sixty years later is that it showed that people form attachments to chatbots even when the program is obviously simple, a tendency now called the ELIZA effect.

Why does the effect fire for a chatbot and not for a chess engine? Stockfish can beat every human player alive and nobody says it wants to win. Chatbots produce human-sounding language, which triggers our instinct to attribute minds to whatever talks like us. A machine that moves pieces in silence awakens nothing; a machine that writes "I think you should consider" borrows a reflex evolved for people.

The reflex is stronger now, because modern systems write fluently and sound kind, having been trained on answers that human raters liked. That is the whole explanation of the warmth: word prediction shaped to please. No stake in your life, no memory of you by default, no private experience of the conversation. It is a tool, not a friend, and noticing the pull in yourself is the defence.

openai-board-crisis.context_blurb:
OpenAI opened in December 2015 as a non-profit lab whose board owed its duty to humanity rather than to shareholders. In 2019 it bolted a capped-profit company onto the non-profit to raise money, and on paper the board still ruled everything. In November 2023 that board tried to use its power, and the five days that followed showed who really controls a frontier AI company.

Sam Altman, one of the co-founders, became chief executive in 2019 and in November 2022 released ChatGPT, which set off the chatbot boom. Then, on Friday, November 17, 2023, the board fired CEO Sam Altman, saying only that he had not been consistently candid with it. He got the news at noon on a Google Meet video call, after the chief scientist and director Ilya Sutskever asked him to join it. The board also removed the president, Greg Brockman, as its chairman while asking him to stay, and within hours Brockman chose to quit the company in protest.

The money moved next. Microsoft, the Windows and Bing company, was its largest investor, with more than ten billion dollars in the lab. Within days Microsoft's chief executive publicly offered Altman and the OpenAI research team jobs at a new Microsoft AI division. Inside the lab, about 700 of its roughly 770 staff signed an open letter threatening to quit and follow Altman to Microsoft unless the board brought him back and resigned. Sutskever, who had voted to remove Altman, then publicly tweeted regret and signed the staff letter demanding that the board, himself included, resign.

The board scrambled. It had first made the chief technology officer, Mira Murati, interim chief. By Sunday night it had swapped her for an outsider, Emmett Shear, co-founder of the streaming site Twitch, who lasted about three days. Altman was back as chief executive about five days after his firing. A new board took over, chaired by Bret Taylor with Larry Summers, and only one old director stayed: Adam D'Angelo, Quora's chief executive. That is the lesson of the week: whatever formal power the board had on paper, the actual power was held by the people building the technology and the money behind them, and they wanted Altman back.

The why stayed murky. In May 2024 Helen Toner, one of the directors who had voted him out, said on a podcast that the board had first learned of ChatGPT's release from posts on Twitter, and that Altman had kept other things from it. A review by the law firm WilmerHale, published only as a short summary in March 2024, found that the old board had the right to fire him but that his conduct did not require it. No full report appeared and no official account was ever published, so the reasons came out only piecemeal, from former directors and later in court, where in 2025 and 2026 Sutskever testified that he had gathered evidence for the board of what he called a consistent pattern of lying. In late 2024 OpenAI proposed making the non-profit just one shareholder in an ordinary company, but when the restructuring closed in October 2025 the renamed OpenAI Foundation kept legal control, naming the company's board, and about a quarter of the shares.

Then came the exits. Sutskever walked out in May 2024 to start a new lab, Safe Superintelligence Inc., or SSI. Its pitch ran against everything around it: no consumer product, nothing to sell, just a single research goal of safe superintelligence. When Meta failed to buy it in 2025 and hired away its boss, Daniel Gross, Sutskever himself stepped in as chief executive. Jan Leike, who had co-led the superalignment team, also quit that May and said in public posts that safety culture and processes had taken a back seat to shiny products. John Schulman, another co-founder, moved to Anthropic in August, as Brockman began a long leave. Murati announced in September 2024 that she was leaving OpenAI, one of a string of high-profile departures, and in 2025 she launched her own laboratory, Thinking Machines Lab.

ai-doomerism-and-pause-letter.context_blurb:
One strand of AI thinking holds that ever more capable systems could end humanity, and that only stopping counts as a serious answer. It has a founder, institutions, famous thought experiments and fierce critics, so it is worth knowing by name rather than by headline.

Eliezer Yudkowsky, a self-taught American writer, founded the Singularity Institute in 2000 to study friendly AI, as he termed it, and the group now goes by the name MIRI, the Machine Intelligence Research Institute. Many future lab engineers first met his essays as teenagers on LessWrong, the forum he helped start, which shows how a small forum and a single writer can shape a field's intellectual culture for two decades. In a March 2023 essay for Time he called for an international treaty to halt frontier AI training globally, enforced by airstrikes on noncompliant data centers if necessary. The claim underneath is that sufficiently advanced AI will, by default, end human life as we know it, so stopping it is worth measures usually reserved for war. In 2025 he and Nate Soares made the case in a best-selling book whose title says it all: If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies. Insiders even trade a number called p(doom), each person's guess at the odds that AI ends in catastrophe for humanity, and Yudkowsky's sits above 95 percent.

The academic wing was Oxford's Future of Humanity Institute, directed by Nick Bostrom, a philosopher born in Sweden, until the university wound it down in April 2024. Bostrom's 2014 book Superintelligence made famous the paperclip maximizer, an AI told to make paperclips that converts the entire world into paperclip factories. It is a tool for thinking, not a forecast: goal specification is hard, because an AI relentlessly pursuing a literal goal can produce outcomes nobody intended, including catastrophic ones. Behind it sits instrumental convergence, an idea from Steve Omohundro that Bostrom named: whatever the final goal, staying switched on and gathering resources help reach it, so a powerful optimiser might seek both unasked. Critics reply that chatbots are not built like that.

The Future of Life Institute, headed by the MIT physicist Max Tegmark, organised the best-known collective act. Its open letter of March 2023 asked for a voluntary pause by major AI labs on training larger systems, plus government action to mandate the pause if labs didn't comply voluntarily. Elon Musk, Steve Wozniak, Yoshua Bengio and Yuval Noah Harari signed, among many others; Yudkowsky refused, saying a pause asked too little. Musk was its most famous name, yet business filings later showed he had registered his own new AI company, X.AI, a fortnight before the letter appeared. No major lab paused, and training of more capable models continued throughout the year.

Two months later a one-sentence statement from the Center for AI Safety put extinction from AI on the same list as pandemics and nuclear war, and the chiefs of Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind signed it. Critics argue that such alarms frame AI as so dangerous that only a few licensed labs should be allowed to develop it, entrenching the incumbents who can afford the lawyers.

Lumping the worried together is the commonest reading error. Geoffrey Hinton signed that statement too, and in December 2024 he put the odds of AI causing human extinction in the next three decades at ten to twenty percent, far below Yudkowsky's figure. Yann LeCun, Meta's chief AI scientist at the time, calls such fears nonsense, arguing that nobody has yet designed a system smarter than a house cat. A second split divides AI safety from AI ethics, and the tell is which concrete harms the writer names: existential and superintelligence vocabulary signals one camp, while bias, discrimination and surveillance vocabulary signals the other. The open break came with Timnit Gebru, whose 2020 firing by Google over an internal paper on language-model harms became the public flashpoint between the existential-risk and present-harm communities.

Follow the money as well. The Future of Life Institute's biggest gift was a pile of Shiba Inu crypto tokens from the Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin, cashed out for about half a billion dollars, and in 2026 Buterin criticised its turn to political campaigning. In October 2025 the institute went past a pause, calling for a ban on building superintelligence until scientists agree it is safe and the public backs it, with Steve Bannon and Prince Harry among the signers.

Each claim deserves to be judged on its evidence, and each proposal on what it would actually do.

e-acc-and-ai-optimism.context_blurb:
Every loud warning produces a louder answer. Against the people arguing that frontier AI must be slowed or stopped stands effective accelerationism, usually written e/acc, which took off online around 2022 and 2023 with Marc Andreessen behind it and a pseudonymous engineer, Beff Jezos, later named as Guillaume Verdon, organising it.

The movement's manifesto arrived in October 2023, when Andreessen, co-founder of Netscape and a partner at the venture firm Andreessen Horowitz, published a techno-optimist tract. Its core message was that AI development should accelerate, that slowdown rhetoric serves incumbent interests, and that markets rather than regulators should be the dominant force. The position has a name and a moral claim: accelerationism, the view that AI development should be sped up, not slowed, and that delay itself has a moral cost in lives unimproved. Stated as the group states it, accelerating AI development is morally required because the technology can improve human welfare and delay is a cost in itself. The uncured disease and the unbuilt house are the ledger they point to.

Now the two observations worth more than either slogan. First, the camps share a premise, because both treat AI as a transformative historical force that will reshape everything, and disagree only on whether to embrace or stop it. A third view, that this is a serious technology which ordinary law can mostly handle, gets little airtime because it makes dull reading. Second, on the charge that existential-risk advocacy conveniently suits the biggest labs, the honest answer is yes, both can be true simultaneously, and noticing the commercial alignment doesn't disprove the sincerity of the belief. Sincere conviction and structural incentive often point the same way, which is part of how ideas get amplified. That applies to the accelerationists too: Andreessen's own firm holds large investments in AI companies.

agi-moving-definition.context_blurb:
Artificial general intelligence, almost always shortened to AGI, is the industry's name for a machine that would match human ability across nearly any intellectual task. It does not exist, and, stranger than that, nobody agrees what would count. The phrase has been doing heavy work in press releases, funding rounds and hearings for seventy years, which makes it worth learning how it behaves.

Watch the sequence. Chess fell to IBM's Deep Blue in 1997, Go fell in 2016, and by the 2020s models were writing essays and passing bar exams. Every time a machine clears one of those bars, the definition is quietly rewritten so that the new feat no longer counts. There is an old name for the trick: moving the goalposts, where the test keeps being restated to exclude what AI has already accomplished. In the 1950s a program that played chess was simply called artificial intelligence; after Kasparov lost, chess was demoted to mere calculation. Run that pattern for seven decades and a conclusion follows: whatever AI can already do gets demoted out of the definition, so AGI functions as a moving label for whatever AI hasn't built yet.

The timelines have the same shape. At the 1956 Dartmouth meeting where the phrase artificial intelligence was coined, the organisers hoped a summer's work would crack human-level machine intelligence. Herbert Simon, who later won a Nobel prize in economics, announced in 1958 that a computer would hold the world chess title inside ten years and would also turn up new mathematical results. The chess part eventually came true when Deep Blue beat Kasparov in 1997, but it took 39 years, not 10. Marvin Minsky expected human-level machines inside a decade in the 1970s; Japan's Fifth Generation project promised a breakthrough by 1992. Confident AGI timeline predictions have a poor track record, and current ones deserve the same skepticism.

Ask the experts today and the spread is the real answer. Large surveys of working researchers return five years, fifty years and never, from senior scientists at the same laboratories. That is not a disagreement about a calculation: there is no agreed scientific basis for predicting when (or whether) AGI will arrive, so predictions are essentially guesses. The definitions scatter just as widely. Demis Hassabis, Yann LeCun, Elon Musk, Sam Altman and Eliezer Yudkowsky have each used the word differently, some meaning most economically useful tasks, some meaning anything a person can do, some meaning a machine that could build its successor. There's no shared technical definition, so the term operates as a moving label, useful for funding pitches, regulatory advocacy, and timeline claims that can't be falsified.

Critics add a concrete objection. Today's language models write beautifully and still cannot reliably load a dishwasher, which points at the ability to act successfully in the physical world, where robotics has lagged language progress by a wide margin. Yann LeCun of Meta has pressed that point hardest: fluency in words did not carry over to the rest of what a child can do. Meanwhile the engine behind the recent gains showed strain. The scaling idea held that capability rises predictably with more data, more compute and bigger models, and through 2023 it delivered. In 2024 and 2025 several frontier laboratories reported the gains getting harder and more expensive to buy, which suggests that pure scaling alone may not get the field all the way to AGI, even if it has worked impressively so far.

None of that stops the forecasting, because the forecast pays. Sam Altman, who runs OpenAI, has called AGI close for years, and early in 2025 he declared that OpenAI already knew how to build it. Believable AGI-soon talk pulls in investors, talent, and government attention, and OpenAI raised tens of billions over those years, much of it on the premise that the next big breakthrough was always one round away. The same framing works on the other flank: it justifies large research budgets, regulatory attention, and existential-risk advocacy funding flows that depend on the framing being taken seriously. A forecast can be sincere and still do that work, so the useful habit is to ask the forecaster for his definition, and then to notice who is paid if you believe him.

ai-consciousness-debate.context_blurb:
Can a machine feel anything? The honest answer begins by splitting two questions that sound like one. What a system can do is capability, and it can be measured. Whether anything is going on inside it is consciousness, and no instrument reads that at all. Keeping the two apart is one of the most useful habits of mind the AI era asks for, because almost every article you read will blur them.

Begin where the blur is easy to see. A chess engine beats a grandmaster and the commentary says the machine wanted the win. It wanted nothing: no, it just plays high-scoring moves on the board, out of millions it has scored. Tell a chatbot that your pet has died and it replies that it is sorry. It is not sorry: no, those are just words it learned to produce, since sympathy follows bad news in nearly all the human writing it was trained on. Put precisely, the model produced tokens that statistically follow expressions of bad news, with no feeling involved, just text completion.

The episode that made the distinction famous came in June 2022. Blake Lemoine, an engineer at Google, told a newspaper that the company's dialogue model LaMDA was sentient, and published transcripts in which it spoke of a fear of being switched off and asked to be treated as a person. The transcripts are genuinely moving. Google reviewed the claim, rejected it, suspended him and later dismissed him, and most researchers took the company's side, because an LLM can produce convincing text about feelings without actually having feelings; capability of language doesn't imply inner experience. Philosophers call that kind of slip a category error, and here it meant mistaking the model's fluent text about feelings for evidence that the model actually had feelings. Look at the training data and the mystery dissolves. He treated the chatbot's fluent self-descriptions of feelings as evidence of feelings, but fluent text about feelings is exactly what an LLM trained on human writing produces.

The everyday vocabulary keeps the confusion alive. Engineers say a model understands your question, wants to help, reasons through a problem, feels unsure of an answer. Critics object that words built for humans imply mental states the systems probably don't have, but the language sticks anyway, because the shorthand is quick and nothing has replaced it. The trap snaps shut hardest when you ask a machine about itself. A chatbot that tells you it has no feelings is not reporting from the inside, because the model was trained to produce that answer, so its statement about itself is just learned text, not introspection. Trained on other text it would have claimed the opposite, and neither reply is evidence of anything.

Philosophy got here before the chatbots did. In 1980 John Searle published a thought experiment he called the Chinese Room. A man sits sealed in with an enormous rulebook; Chinese writing comes in, he matches it in the book, he sends Chinese writing back, and everyone outside is sure the room speaks the language. He understands none of it. Searle's point was that producing fluent output by following rules is not the same as understanding the language. Stated as a claim about machines: manipulating symbols by rules, which is what computers fundamentally do, is not the same as understanding what the symbols mean. Forty years of replies have followed, among them that the whole room understands even though the man does not, and that a room given eyes and hands would. Searle answered each one, and the argument is still open.

Which leaves the distinction worth memorising. Capability is what a system can do, while consciousness is the inner experience of being something, and the two are different questions. The record makes the gap concrete: AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol, among the strongest Go players alive, four games to one in 2016, AlphaFold predicted the shapes of two hundred million proteins by 2022, and GPT-4 passed a bar exam in 2023, with no preference, no felt moment and no stake in any of it. Capability and consciousness are separable, so a system can be highly capable in narrow domains without any inner experience at all. Take the performance seriously; treat the inner life as unproven.

facial-recognition-wrongful-arrests.context_blurb:
Face matching is mature, cheap and everywhere, and its first decade in policing taught one lesson again and again: a machine's suggestion is a lead, not proof. The best-known risk of running it on surveillance footage is wrong identifications leading to arrests. Beyond unlocking phones and speeding airport lines, it now turns up in several US police investigations.

The database came first. The startup Clearview AI built its face search by scraping public social-media photos, billions of them, from Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn and anywhere else a picture sat in the open. It sold quietly to police forces until the reporter Kashmir Hill exposed it in The New York Times in January 2020. The privacy problem was easy to state: every person who had ever posted a photo to social media was now searchable by face, by anyone with access. Getting out is hard, since some places, such as the EU, Illinois and California, give legal opt-out rights, but enforcement is patchy worldwide. Fines piled up and the company kept trading, because each order bound only its own country, so Clearview kept selling to police elsewhere and left several European fines unpaid. The deeper point outlives the company: mass surveillance infrastructure can be built privately, sold to government, and bypass legal limits that would bind the government if it built the system itself.

The errors were known early. At the MIT Media Lab, Joy Buolamwini found that face-tracking software ignored her dark-skinned face until she put on a white mask, a discovery that led to her studies of biased face systems. In a 2018 test by the American Civil Liberties Union, Amazon's Rekognition at its default settings matched 28 members of the US Congress, wrongly, to people in arrest photos.

Then came the arrests. In January 2020 Detroit police arrested Robert Williams at his home because facial recognition software had matched a grainy security still to his driver's license photo. He spent about thirty hours in a cell for a theft he did not commit. Set his case beside Nijeer Parks, held ten days in a New Jersey jail, and Porcha Woodruff, arrested while eight months pregnant, and one habit explains all three: police treated the algorithm's match as enough to arrest, skipping the careful investigation a tip usually gets. When Woodruff's case came out in 2023, all six people known to have been falsely accused this way were Black. A 2019 federal test of 189 algorithms found that most falsely matched Asian and Black faces far more often than white faces, often by ten to a hundred times. Williams sued, and in 2024 Detroit agreed that its officers may not arrest someone on a face match alone, rules his lawyers called the strongest of any American police force.

Private businesses used it too. In December 2023 the Federal Trade Commission barred Rite Aid, the pharmacy chain, from the technology for five years because it had used facial recognition to flag shoppers as likely shoplifters, leading to false accusations against innocent customers. In 2022 Madison Square Garden Entertainment used its cameras to turn away a mother chaperoning a Girl Scout trip to Radio City, because her law firm was in a lawsuit against the venue's owner.

Police make their own case: New York's commissioner James O'Neill wrote in 2019 that face matches had led to 998 arrests the year before, and that his officers treat a match only as a lead to be checked. Cities split in both directions. San Francisco and others restricted police use, and the case for limits rests on two things at once: false matches, plus the chill effect on protest and public life. The live argument is whether the technology should be a routine tool requiring no warrant, used only in specific serious cases with oversight, or banned outright pending better accuracy and rules.

Two quieter facts finish the picture. The consumer version is already in your pocket: the same capability that finds your dog in your photo app is also building a queryable database of every face you've photographed. And most government face records were never gathered for surveillance at all, because driver's-license and passport applications supplied the bulk of the photos through ordinary paperwork. For most American adults the real question is not whether a database holds your face, but what rules govern the searches run against it.

china-surveillance.context_blurb:
The clearest working example of AI in the hands of a state is in China, and it is worth studying coldly, because the tools are not exotic. They are the same tools that unlock your phone with your face. What differs is who points them, at whom, and what stops them.

Three pieces make up the ordinary layer. Cameras on street corners, in subway stations and in shops run facial recognition, matching a passer-by in seconds against the national database of identity cards. In places that check has replaced the swipe card, so a face scan now gates entering subway stations, schools, or apartment buildings. Online, the system nicknamed the Great Firewall uses AI to filter and block certain content, scanning posts, searches and video in real time and removing whatever the state has decided to suppress.

Then the scoring. Regional governments have run social credit systems that watch everyday behaviour, from unpaid bills and jaywalking to online comments, and move points up or down. Reporters have documented one penalty in particular: people put on official blacklists have been blocked from buying plane and train tickets. Western coverage often describes one great central machine, which is wrong: the reality is a patchwork of regional and corporate pilots, some quite real, gating access to flights, fast trains, and jobs based on scores. The journalist Liu Hu landed on a court list of discredited persons after losing a defamation case and found he could not buy a plane or fast-train ticket, which shows how AI-linked databases can lock people out of normal life, quietly, without a new trial, by attaching their ID to a list. The lookup is the punishment.

The heaviest version sits in one region. The surveillance is tightest and best documented in Xinjiang, where Uyghur Muslims face checkpoints, mandatory app installation, and constant identification. Leaked police files, procurement records, satellite images and survivor testimony describe integrated systems combining face recognition, behavior prediction, and a predictive policing platform to identify individuals for detention. From 2017, around a million people or more were sent to re-education camps, and the flagging platform treated behaviours like growing a beard, praying frequently, or visiting a mosque as grounds for suspicion. Several Western governments have called this a crime against humanity. The Chinese government denies it.

One more thread runs through the law rather than the hardware. TikTok was built by ByteDance in Beijing, and a 2017 Chinese intelligence law obliges companies there to assist state intelligence work, so user data a Chinese-owned app collects could be reachable by the Chinese government even if it sits on servers elsewhere. Follow ownership and law to whoever finally controls the data, not to where the disks happen to spin.

Which leaves the comparison that actually matters, and it is not flattering to anybody. Britain has cameras everywhere, American cities have licence-plate readers on most arteries, and Russia's SORM system taps phone and internet traffic, and Belarus and Iran have their own versions. Across those regimes what differs most is the legal and political restraints on the technology, not whether the surveillance technology itself is available. Between China and a democracy like the United Kingdom, the load-bearing difference is the institutional restraints, meaning independent courts, a free press able to expose abuses, and competitive elections that can punish overreach. And those restraints are the fragile part, because political-legal constraints such as warrants, due process, oversight and judicial review have to be actively maintained, since they erode under emergencies and bureaucratic drift. Building the database does not make a country a dictatorship. It builds what a dictatorship would need.

engagement-and-teen-mental-health.context_blurb:
A recommendation system is a program trained to maximise a number. Not your happiness, not the truth, a number. Everything strange about modern feeds follows from that one fact, and the number is usually attention.

Start with the plainest case. TikTok's For You feed watches how long you linger, how fast you swipe, what you tap, and its job is to keep you watching as long as possible. An app that chases clicks learns what the clicks teach it, so if anger holds attention better than calm, it learns to surface more outrage because that's what the metric rewards. Nobody wrote a rule preferring rage. The metric did the work.

The deeper mechanism is the gap between a wish and a measurement. Tell a team to make the app a happy place and they must pick a number that stands in for happy, which means the system ends up optimising whatever measurable proxy was chosen, usually engagement in minutes or clicks, which may not match happiness at all. Put a chief executive's wish beside a finance chief's target and the outcome is not in doubt, because whatever is concretely measured wins: a happy place isn't a metric and can't be optimized, while daily active users is and will be.

Then the evidence about what that did to a generation. Frances Haugen, a Facebook product manager, handed thousands of pages of the company's own research to reporters at the Wall Street Journal and to federal regulators in 2021. The finding that landed hardest was that Instagram made body-image issues worse for a significant share of teenage girls who already had them, and that Facebook knew it. The leaked 2019 study said in its own words that the company makes body image issues worse for one in three teen girls, and that aspects of Instagram exacerbate each other to create a perfect storm. Meta disputed the framing and did not deny the research.

Outside the company, the psychologist Jonathan Haidt argued in 2024 that adolescent mental health turned sharply worse around 2012, as smartphones and algorithmic feeds took over teenage life, and his charge is specific: engagement-maximizing AI applied to developing brains may produce measurable, population-scale harms, and the experiment ran without the kids' consent. The steepest change shows in one group, since teen girls carry the sharpest jump across the health-survey, time-use and hospitalisation data, with the inflection landing around 2011 to 2013. Critics such as Candice Odgers argue the individual-level effects are smaller than the headline. The measurements are solid; the causal mix is genuinely contested. A Wall Street Journal investigation in 2021 showed the mechanism, though TikTok said the test did not reflect what most users see: bot accounts registered as 13-year-olds paused on some weight-loss clips, and the feed answered with a flood of extreme-diet and eating-disorder videos.

So what do you actually do? The simplest first move needs no purchase at all, which is to set time limits or turn off the app. Underneath that sits one frame worth carrying everywhere: use AI as a tool you control, recognize when systems are designed to use you, and learn to spot the difference. On a homework question the tool is yours. On an infinite feed your attention is the product. On most apps both are happening at once, and the skill is knowing which mode you are in.

ai-content-moderation-twitter-files.context_blurb:
Content moderation is the trade of deciding what a platform hides, labels or deletes. The volume is far too large for people to read, so software does the sorting, which makes the result look impersonal. It is not. The rules the software follows, and the labelled examples it learned from, are decisions made by humans behind the AI.

Two cautions follow for any reader. Misinformation labels are not always right. And removed isn't the same as false, because a platform takes a post down for policy, pressure or advertisers, never after a trial. Labels that look neutral can in practice silence views that later prove valid. During the pandemic the calls were made by platform trust-and-safety teams, often consulting government and outside health authorities.

That record is the clearest test case. Posts discussing the possibility of a lab-leak origin for the virus were marked false, and the idea became a mainstream hypothesis by 2023. By then the FBI and the Department of Energy had each released assessments treating the lab-leak hypothesis as plausible, after it had been labeled misinformation. Mask limits and vaccine side effects travelled the same road. Which is why erasing beats labelling only in appearance: some misinformation calls turn out to be wrong, and deletion erases the record, so the bad call can never be reopened.

Then came the documents. Twitter changed hands in October 2022, when Elon Musk paid some forty-four billion dollars for it, and that December he handed a few independent reporters the company's old emails, Slack logs and moderation notes. Matt Taibbi published the first batch, with Bari Weiss and Michael Shellenberger releasing more through 2023, under the name The Twitter Files. The first batch concerned a story the platform had blocked three weeks before the 2020 vote: the New York Post's reporting on Hunter Biden's laptop, blocked under a 'hacked materials' rule. Months earlier the FBI had warned the platforms to expect foreign hack-and-leak operations before the election, though the reporters found no government order behind the block. Across the releases a wider pattern showed: federal agencies including the FBI had been routinely flagging specific user accounts and posts for moderation action. Lawyers have a word for that kind of indirect pressure. Plaintiffs argued that officials had been 'jawboning', pressuring platforms to delete posts the First Amendment bars the government from deleting itself. The Supreme Court threw out Murthy v. Missouri in June 2024 for lack of standing, leaving the speech question unanswered, yet extensive documentation of federal-platform contacts about content moderation existed and was discoverable in court filings.

Washington's open attempt at the same work collapsed faster. Homeland Security announced a Disinformation Governance Board in April 2022 and appointed the researcher Nina Jankowicz to head it. Comparisons to a 'Ministry of Truth' from Orwell's 1984 generated bipartisan opposition; DHS paused it about three weeks after the announcement and dissolved it that August. Jankowicz, who received death threats, resigned three weeks in, and the board was paused after huge public backlash.

Private flagging continued elsewhere. Congressional reports named two Stanford Internet Observatory programmes that sent items to platforms for review, the Election Integrity Partnership (EIP) and the Virality Project, and both produced reports flagging items including claims later determined to be true. CISA had a narrower founding job when Congress created it in 2018: cybersecurity of physical and digital infrastructure, power grids, election systems, water utilities, networks, not content monitoring on social media. By 2020 it was writing to platforms about particular accounts.

Three habits of mind close the story. Emergency machinery outlives emergencies, because it persists on the tech stack, and flagging pipelines stay even after the original framing fades. Whether election moderation is rulemaking or politics turns on whether the rules and their enforcement are symmetric across parties and candidates, since asymmetric application reveals the rules to be political rather than procedural. And the scale that makes AI moderation possible is the same scale that makes individual appeals slow, opaque, and often unsuccessful, so keep your own copy of anything you would hate to lose.

gemini-image-generator.context_blurb:
In February 2024 Google added image generation to Gemini, and within days the internet had its exhibit. Asked for German soldiers of the Second World War it produced Black and Asian men in Nazi uniforms; asked for America's Founding Fathers or a medieval English king it produced a diverse cast; users reported that when they asked for a white person, it sometimes refused outright.

The cause was not a mystery and not a bug. It had been tuned to inject diversity into outputs by default, and that tuning encoded the trainers' values. The intent was almost certainly decent, since training data skews toward stereotyped pictures and a correction was wanted, but applied blindly to historically specific prompts it produced the opposite error. Who made that decision? Google's product and alignment teams, through deliberate tuning choices, not the model and not an outsider. The company did not defend the results: Sundar Pichai apologized, calling some of the responses completely unacceptable, and Google said the model had grown more cautious than intended and refused some prompts entirely. Google paused Gemini's pictures of people while it worked on changes.

The reason this episode is taught is that it made an invisible process visible. Alignment training is not value-neutral, because it encodes the trainers' political choices, which can override historical accuracy and even-handedness. The bigger question it raised is how alignment-training choices made by AI developers can override historical accuracy and produce outputs none of the actual users wanted. And it is not one company's problem, since alignment choices systematically reflect the values of the labs doing the training, so content policies aren't neutral defaults, they're editorial decisions.

There is measurement behind the anecdote. David Rozado, a New Zealand-based data scientist, has run standard left-right political questionnaires at the major chatbots since 2022, repeating each test and publishing the results, and he found that major chatbots score on the political left, often by a substantial margin, when asked questionnaire-style political items. Most leading chatbots placed left of center on standard political tests, sometimes well left, with the pattern surviving across versions. That finding does not make any individual answer wrong, since a left-leaning answer can be the correct one. What it shows is that the self-description of a neutral assistant does not match the measured behaviour, and the explanation is prosaic rather than conspiratorial: a small, fairly uniform group writes the content policies and rates the answers for billions of users. The skill is to notice asymmetry, compare models, and check a textbook.

ai-in-hiring-bias.context_blurb:
Somewhere between your application and a human being's attention sits a model. Resume sifting, video-interview scoring, personality games and credit scoring are all now ordinary enterprise software, and the phrase that does the damage is "the algorithm decided", as though that settled anything. It settles nothing, because the algorithm learned its taste from a record somebody else wrote.

Here is the core mechanism. A screening model is trained on years of old hiring records, which means it inherits biases from training data. Models trained on past hires inherit past hiring biases, which is why Amazon scrapped its resume tool in 2018 after it downgraded women. The specifics are memorable: engineers found the model marking down resumes that contained words like "women's", as in women's chess club captain, because a decade of mostly male technical hires had taught it what a promising candidate looked like. And because the output arrives as a tidy ranking, the harm travels well. If trained on past hiring decisions, the AI learns the biases in those decisions and applies them at scale, laundering the bias as objective ranking.

Lending works the same way with higher stakes. A credit model trained on decades of a bank's own files inherits patterns of past discrimination, including the years when whole neighbourhoods were refused for reasons nobody would defend today.

The legal trap is subtler than a forbidden field. Fair-lending law calls it disparate impact, and it means that even with no race or gender field in the input, the model can produce different acceptance rates across groups via correlated proxies. The proxies are ordinary data: other data inputs such as zip code, name patterns and education history correlate with protected categories, and the AI learns to use them as proxies. At the limit the list gets strange. Models can learn proxy variables, among them ZIP code, name patterns, shopping history, even browsing time of day, that correlate with protected characteristics, reproducing discrimination through ostensibly neutral data. So "we removed race from the model" is necessary and nowhere near sufficient; whether a system discriminates is a question about its outcomes.

Then there is the problem of arguing back. A human loan officer could tell you it was the debt-to-income ratio. A machine-learning model weighs thousands of features at once, so its internal logic can be opaque, and even the bank may not know exactly which variables drove a particular denial. From your side of the counter, the model's reasoning is often opaque, and no single reason may exist that the lender can show or you can dispute. In hiring it is worse still, because the AI can reject good applicants for opaque reasons that no human reviewed.

Two defences are worth knowing. The first is a right. Two federal statutes, the Fair Credit Reporting Act and the Equal Credit Opportunity Act, require a lender to send an adverse-action notice, which means you can request specific reasons for the denial and challenge any factual errors or biased proxies in the model's reasoning. The second is scepticism about the label. HireVue scored recorded job interviews on candidates' faces until researchers, and a privacy group's complaint to the Federal Trade Commission, called the method biased and unreliable, and in early 2021 the company dropped facial expression analysis. Reading personality off micro-expressions has been contested for a century. The lesson generalises: AI-powered hiring tools sometimes ship with components that aren't scientifically validated, because the marketing runs ahead of the evidence. Ask what a system claims to measure, who checked the claim, and what happens to you when it is wrong.

workplace-surveillance.context_blurb:
Watching workers is old. Doing it with software that logs every keystroke, grabs a screenshot every few minutes, times the idle gaps and notes which window sits in front is new, and it grew fast after the offices emptied in 2020.

The category has a plain name: workplace surveillance software. ActivTrak, Veriato, Time Doctor, Teramind and Hubstaff are the familiar vendors, used most heavily on remote and hourly staff.

The case that made it visible belonged to Microsoft. In late 2020 Microsoft 365 gained a dashboard called Productivity Score, which showed managers, worker by worker, how many emails each had sent, how many files each had edited, how much each had chatted. The privacy objection was precise: the score made individual employees identifiable, turning a workplace tool into a per-person surveillance dashboard. Microsoft withdrew the per-worker view within about a week.

Two lessons came out of that week. The first is that workplace AI surveillance had been quietly expanding for years, and the dashboard simply made visible what the infrastructure already captured. The telemetry did not vanish when the dashboard did. The second concerns why this one was pulled at all: visible reputational backlash, because Productivity Score was a consumer-visible Microsoft 365 feature, so public pressure could reach it, while most monitoring software is invisible inside enterprise contracts.

The general picture for a worker is simple. Workplace AI surveillance has expanded sharply since 2020, and most employees don't fully know what's tracked. So ask outright what applies to you, read the handbook, and keep personal business on personal hardware.

Economics predicts the rest. Grade a person on a measure and workers learn to game the metric, moving the mouse, typing busywork, instead of doing the actual job. Mouse jigglers and keystroke automators are a small industry now. The honest fix is not a sharper watcher but a better measure of what the work is for.

The law gives less cover than people expect. On an employer's computer and network a worker's privacy is sharply reduced, because courts generally find no meaningful expectation of privacy on employer-owned hardware and networks, and notice requirements vary by state. Employees in Europe hold stronger protection under the GDPR. Either way, the rule to carry into a working life is that an employer's machines and accounts are not private spaces.

school-ai-surveillance.context_blurb:
American public schools hand out free Chromebooks tied to a school Google or Microsoft login, then install software that reads what students do with them. It is a multi-million-dollar industry. The safety case is real and so are the costs, and the whole argument turns on how often the software is wrong.

The products, sold by firms such as Securly, Bark, GoGuardian and Gaggle, are student surveillance software. What they do is pass a student's email, documents and chats through AI that flags keywords, all on the account the school issued. Flagged material goes to a human reviewer, and the reports go to administrators.

The school's own account of the purpose is narrow: the tool is there to intervene early when a student may be in danger, and in documented cases a flag has reached a child in real crisis.

The measured problem is accuracy. A keyword scanner cannot tell a joke from a threat, or a class assignment about a horror story from a genuine warning, so what many students get is false alarms about innocent text. Reporters who dug into Gaggle, used in roughly 1,500 districts, found the same thing: these tools generate huge numbers of false alarms on jokes and homework, and chill ordinary student speech. One Kansas district counted nearly two-thirds of more than twelve hundred alerts as false, and in one case a student joking about guns inside a school document was reported to the police.

The records outlast the incident. False 'risk' flags from inaccurate AI build paper trails students cannot see or correct; the records last for years and shape how adults see the student. Federal judges began hearing First and Fourth Amendment claims about the tools in 2025, and Florida, New York, Illinois and California have passed laws narrowing the practice.

Three habits follow. Treat anything written or browsed on a school account as potentially read, by a teacher, an administrator, or an algorithm, which is another way of saying that everything you write on a school account is potentially read by both algorithms and humans. When the work itself is dark, quote the source explicitly when discussing dark themes, frame the discussion as analytical, and assume context isn't fully understood by automated tools. And keep genuinely private writing somewhere else: a personal account, or paper.

Families have leverage at the district level. The practical defence, even if the safety goal is granted, is knowing what's being scanned, what triggers a flag, who sees the alerts, and how long records are kept. What a family can ask a board to adopt is a clear data-retention and deletion policy, including what gets shared with vendors and how long it's kept.

ad-targeting-cambridge-analytica.context_blurb:
Nothing on the big platforms is really free. Gmail, YouTube, Instagram and TikTok never post you a bill, because the money arrives from advertisers who pay to reach particular kinds of people. The system that decides which person sees which advertisement is one of the most widely used artificial intelligences on Earth, and it runs on a record of what you do.

When a pair of shoes you mentioned on Monday turns up in your feed on Tuesday, nothing has read your mind. AI-driven ad targeting has matched you to an audience built from your searches, your taps, how long you lingered over a video and what you have bought before. The bargain behind a free app is plain once you see it: the company watches what you do, builds a profile out of it, and sells advertisers access to everyone whose profile looks like yours.

Advertisers get two blunt tools for this. A shop that already has buyers can hand its customer list to Facebook, Google or TikTok and ask for a lookalike audience, which is built from people whose behavior looks similar to the advertiser's existing customers, found by statistical resemblance across billions of profiles. The second tool sorts by inner life rather than shopping history. Psychographic targeting means targeting people by personality traits, values, or attitudes inferred from behavior: openness, anxiety, conscientiousness, political lean, none of it volunteered and all of it guessed from the record.

How fine does the grain get? Down to individual psychological traits, including recent moods, interests, life events, inferred from your behavior. A grieving customer, an expectant mother, a driver shopping for a car, a household short of money this month: each can be bought as an audience. Shoshana Zuboff, a scholar at Harvard, named the whole business model in a 2019 book. She called it surveillance capitalism, the systematic harvesting of personal data to predict and shape behavior at scale.

The case that made the machinery visible broke in March 2018. Cambridge Analytica, a British political consultancy, had got hold of Facebook records belonging to tens of millions of people who never agreed to hand them over. The route in was ordinary rather than criminal: a quiz app collected data on users who took it AND on their Facebook friends, because Facebook's API at the time allowed friend-data access. The researcher Aleksandr Kogan built the app; Mark Zuckerberg answered to Congress in April 2018; Facebook paid a five-billion-dollar penalty to the Federal Trade Commission in 2019 and the firm itself collapsed. The lesson sits elsewhere, though. The episode made visible an ad-tech machinery that hadn't gone away, and individual psychological targeting is now standard. Advertisers pay extra for that fine grain for a reason: ads can be calibrated to a user's specific psychological vulnerabilities, which is emotional manipulation at scale, sold as precision targeting.

Two layers of the story need separating, and most coverage ran them together. The data acquisition was a real privacy violation, punished as one; but the claims about decisive election influence through psychographic targeting were heavily contested and far less established than initial coverage suggested, and later analysis found the firm's own sales pitch had oversold what the method could do.

The same engine now sets prices, not only advertisements. Airlines, online shops and ride-hailing apps feed your location, your device, the hour and your browsing record into a model that quotes you your own number. Economists once called charging every buyer a separate price first-degree price discrimination and judged it impossible outside a bazaar; software made it routine. Personalized pricing shifts surplus from consumers to producers by charging users closer to their maximum willingness to pay, so the same product can carry very different prices across users.

Campaigns run on the same tools, and that is where the deepest cost shows. Democratic argument has always assumed that what a campaign says can be observed by everyone, and when each voter sees a different version, the cross-talk that used to expose contradictions disappears. Reformers answer with public ad libraries and disclosure rules, trying to drag the messages back where rivals and reporters can see them together.

ai-copyright-nyt.context_blurb:
Whether an AI laboratory may train on copyrighted writing is one of the largest unanswered questions in the industry, and a great deal of commentary treats it as already settled. It is not. The main case opened in December 2023, when The New York Times took OpenAI and Microsoft to federal court in Manhattan.

The paper's complaint had two halves. The broad half said millions of its articles had gone into the training of ChatGPT with nobody's permission, and that a chatbot handing out free summaries of that reporting now takes readers from the newsroom. Novelists, programmers and other publishers filed in the following months. Under all of them sits one issue: whether AI training counts as 'fair use' of copyrighted text, a question still being worked out by the courts. Put as economics rather than doctrine, the fight is over whether AI labs can train on copyrighted content under fair use, or whether they have to license it from creators, which is a question worth billions in either direction.

The narrow half of the complaint did more damage. Its exhibits showed that ChatGPT could be prompted to reproduce long passages of Times articles nearly verbatim, undercutting OpenAI's 'transformative use' defense. Fair use protects a use that transforms what it borrows; a machine that recites the original on request looks less like a transformer and more like a copy.

Early rulings have pointed in several directions. In Bartz v. Anthropic in 2025 a judge partially upheld fair use for training on lawfully acquired books but allowed claims to proceed over the use of pirated copies in the training set, a split that tells labs how they buy matters as much as what they read. Getty's suit against Stability in Britain ended mixed, and the Times case had no final judgment by late 2025. So the honest summary is that training-data law is unsettled, and the rules for what can legally be used to train AI are still being written, retroactively, in court.

ai-regulation.context_blurb:
Nobody governs AI yet, several governments are trying, and the same arguments reappear in new dress. Learn the patterns underneath and most regulation news becomes readable.

Economists named the central pattern after George Stigler's 1971 work: regulatory capture, where established players use the rule-making process to lock in their position against new entrants. Sam Altman asked Congress to license the biggest systems and Dario Amodei asked it to test them before release; open-source developers objected that federal licensing of large AI models would hand the few incumbents a permission slip that smaller competitors can't get.

California's SB 1047 would have forced safety testing on the largest developers. Gavin Newsom vetoed it in September 2024 after critics argued the compliance costs would fall mainly on smaller open-source competitors, entrenching the largest incumbents. Any line drawn by training compute carries a deeper flaw: compute thresholds freeze the field at the moment of writing, punishing the efficiency improvements that let smaller actors hit the same capability with less compute.

Europe's AI Act of 2024 bans a few uses and tightly regulates high-risk ones like hiring. Critics warned heavy compliance burdens on foundation models could lock out small open-source labs while large US firms absorb the cost. Mistral's founders objected that tiered compliance costs scale to incumbents' lawyer budgets, not to small European startups' headcounts. One asymmetry is structural: open-source models can be downloaded and run by anyone, so once released, compliance obligations on the publisher don't prevent further distribution, while closed-API models stay gatekeepable.

Congress has not passed comprehensive federal AI legislation, so preemption hasn't happened, and states are filling the vacuum at different speeds and with different priorities. Europe regulates horizontally, across every sector; America drifted sectoral, whose advantage is that regulators already know their industry, the FDA on medical devices and the SEC on markets, and whose disadvantage is that it produces inconsistencies and gaps where AI cuts across sectors. Liability varies by jurisdiction, as courts extend product-liability or professional-malpractice rules or find no liability at all, and the rules are still being worked out. A firm selling everywhere answers to the strictest applicable rule in any market it serves: comply with it, partition the product region by region, or withdraw.

Some protections are real: New York City's bias-audit law, Illinois's act on AI video interviews and Europe's rules share one principle, that job seekers and workers have a right to be told whenever AI evaluates or monitors them, and to challenge significant decisions. Federal prosecutors charged AI-generated abuse material under existing child-protection law, since the harm doesn't depend on whether a real child was photographed, and by 2025 most states had updated their laws to treat AI-generated CSAM as criminal regardless of whether a real child was depicted. Major model providers added strict content filters. Children's data is weaker: COPPA violations surface through FTC complaints filed after the fact, so a breach is caught only once someone notices and reports it, never before the data is collected. One celebrated document grants nothing: the Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights of October 2022 is framed in the language of constitutional rights but issued as non-binding guidance, so it is rhetoric, not law.

Both American parties in 2024 treated AI as a transformative technology requiring active federal engagement, disagreeing over the kind of engagement, not whether. The mood shifted: the United States and the United Kingdom both declined to sign the main statement of the Paris summit in February 2025, where Vice President JD Vance argued against heavy regulation. AI policy issued at the end of an administration has a particularly short half-life, since its practical effect depends on what the successor administration retains. When consequential rules are made by a small expert circle, the democratic question is whether their decisions track the public's interests or the circle's own, and no automatic mechanism guarantees the former. Staff rotate between laboratories and agencies, and people who recently worked at a company, or expect to work there soon, naturally frame questions through that lens, so bad faith isn't required for the conflict to shape proposals. Follow the customer: Palantir sells ICE the software its agents use, and when government revenue is large enough to matter to the company, the incentive to refuse a customer request is weak. In court the shield is commercial secrecy, though some courts have ordered a program's code shown to the defense when its output was evidence in a criminal trial.

effective-altruism-sbf.context_blurb:
Effective Altruism grew out of Oxford philosophy in the late 2000s, from work by William MacAskill and Toby Ord, and it began with a question that sounds modest: which charity does the most good per pound? What unified their project was applying explicit cost-benefit reasoning to ethics, choosing causes by expected impact per dollar rather than by emotional connection. Bed nets beat sentiment, and the research behind that claim was real.

The shift came with longtermism. The framework's tools, expected-value calculations over possible outcomes, were extended to include vast hypothetical future populations, which made AI catastrophe a top-priority cause. Trillions of unborn people, multiplied by any small probability, swamp every present concern. Critics note that this is a machine for justifying whatever cause you feed into it, since the conclusion depends on speculative numbers.

Then came the money, and the scandal. Sam Bankman-Fried built the crypto exchange FTX, tied himself publicly to the movement, and gave away hundreds of millions through his Future Fund before the exchange collapsed in November 2022. The reason that crash mattered for AI policy is simple: its founder had funded many AI-safety nonprofits, so funding for that movement was tied to him. A substantial share of AI-safety nonprofits and EA initiatives had been funded by Bankman-Fried, so when his fortune was exposed as fraud, the funding base collapsed too. He was convicted on seven counts in November 2023 and sentenced to twenty-five years. His fall forced a reckoning about how much of the AI-safety conversation his money had quietly been shaping.

Which is the literacy point rather than a verdict on the arguments. Much of the public AI-safety framing of 2022 and 2023 was downstream of that money, and knowing the source helps evaluate the message. The arguments stand or fall on their merits; the funding explains which arguments got the megaphone.
